timezone_note: Armenia has a single time zone and does not observe daylight saving time; the WMO's country record for Armenia, supplied by the national Hydrometeorology and Monitoring Center SNCO, lists Yerevan at UTC+04:00 with DST flagged 'N'. This agrees with the IANA zone Asia/Yerevan.
passport_validity_rule: Armenia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs states only that a foreigner must hold a valid passport (plus a visa or residency document where one is required) to enter; it publishes no minimum number of months of remaining validity. The UK FCDO, describing the same rule, says a passport 'must be valid for the duration of your stay'. There is no six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: Nationals of countries under Armenia's unilateral visa-free regime may stay up to 180 days in any one-year period unless an international agreement sets a different term (MFA). Nationals of a further list of countries are also visa-exempt if they hold a valid residence permit issued by the USA, an EU/Schengen state, the UAE, Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait or Oman that is valid for at least six months from the date of entry; the permit must be shown as a physical card or as a sticker in the passport (Armenian Embassy in Kuwait, mfa.am). Nationals who are not exempt can apply for an e-visa at evisa.mfa.am. The FCDO notes strict customs rules on goods taken into and out of Armenia, and that entry is refused to anyone without a valid travel document or using a passport reported lost or stolen. No official source consulted states a proof-of-funds, onward-ticket, insurance or arrival-card requirement, so none is recorded here.

health.notes: The US CDC's destination page for Armenia states that yellow fever vaccine is 'not required' for country entry and 'not recommended' by CDC, so nothing is checked at the border on health grounds. The remaining vaccines are advisory only. CDC lists no malaria risk for Armenia. Armenia's own health ministry was not used as a source here; this is the CDC's assessment.

money.card_acceptance: Armenia's official tourism board says credit cards are widely accepted in Yerevan, but the country remains largely cash-dependent outside the capital.
money.cash_culture: Carry cash for markets, restaurants and rural areas; the Yerevan metro runs on a 100 AMD coin/token system and is cash only, and taxis are best paid in cash (armenia.travel).
money.tipping: Armenia's official tourism board says it is customary to leave a 10% tip when dining out.
money.atm_notes: ATMs are plentiful in Yerevan, and currency-exchange offices plus kiosks in some major supermarkets are widely available (armenia.travel). No official source was found on ATM fees or dynamic-currency-conversion practice, so none is stated.

power.adapter_note: Armenia's official tourism board describes sockets as primarily Type C (European standard) at 220-240V, and says a device labelled 'INPUT: 100-240V, 50/60 Hz' needs only a Type C adaptor. Travellers from a 230V country therefore need a plug adaptor but no voltage converter. Supply frequency is not stated by any official source consulted, so it is left null.

emergency.notes: Armenia's official tourism board lists 911 as the Emergency Situations Crisis Management Center line alongside the direct services (fire 101, police 102, ambulance 103, gas emergency 104, Yerevan municipality 105, airport hotline 187). Armenia's Rescue Service (rescue.mia.gov.am, Ministry of Internal Affairs) also refers to 911 as the country's emergency number. No official source consulted confirms that the EU-standard 112 connects in Armenia, so it is not recorded; dial 911 or the direct three-digit numbers. No official source states which languages are answered.

getting_around.summary: Yerevan has a metro that runs on a 100 AMD coin/token system (cash only) plus buses and minibuses, and taxis and ride-hailing are cheap and widely used — the official tourism board names GG and Yandex Taxi as the main apps. For timetables the tourism board points visitors at the T-armenia.com app, which covers both Yerevan and national transport services, and at the A2B Yerevan public-transport listing; Yandex Maps is recommended for navigation and Yerevan Ride for bike sharing. Outside Yerevan, carry cash.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Armenia's official tourism board says SIM cards are very accessible and affordable and can be bought at the airport or from providers in the city, with widespread coverage in both cities and rural areas. It does not state what identification is required to register a SIM, and no official source was found that does.
connectivity.typical_cost: The official tourism board states plans can be bought for up to about USD 12 per month including unlimited data, SMS and domestic and international calls (checked 2026-09-28). No official per-10GB or two-week price is published.

timezone_note: Colombia uses a single time zone across the mainland and the island department of San Andres, Providencia and Santa Catalina, and does not observe daylight saving time.
passport_validity_rule: Colombia requires only that the passport be valid on the date of entry; there is no stated minimum validity beyond that. The UK FCDO records that Colombian immigration authorities nonetheless recommend an expiry date at least 6 months after the date you plan to leave, and airlines may apply their own margin at check-in.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa-exempt visitors are admitted for up to 90 days for tourism or business at the immigration officer's discretion, extendable to 120 days and capped at 180 days in any 12-month period (UK FCDO). An onward or return ticket valid within the 90-day period must be producible, and Migracion Colombia's own travel-requirements page also lists proof of economic solvency alongside the passport and any required visa. CHECK-MIG: Migracion Colombia operates an online pre-registration form, Check-Mig, for travellers entering AND leaving Colombia, completed between 72 hours and 1 hour before travel (https://apps.migracioncolombia.gov.co/pre-registro/). Two official sources describe its status differently and both are worth knowing: Migracion Colombia presents it as the pre-registration step for anyone intending to enter or exit, while the UK FCDO states plainly that completing it 'is not mandatory' and that it exists to speed up entry. Migracion Colombia's travel-requirements page also indicates Check-Mig is not presented at land border posts. Practical reading: fill it in before each flight, and do not treat a missing form as a bar to boarding. Separately, travellers flying to San Andres, Providencia or Santa Catalina must buy a tourist card at the boarding gate on the day of the flight unless staying under 24 hours (UK FCDO).

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever certificate if arriving from a country with yellow fever transmission risk (see notes - official sources disagree on how broadly this applies)
recommended_vaccinations: Typhoid (rural travel or stays of a month or more)
Yellow fever (for travel to at-risk departments and municipalities, given at least 10 days before arrival there)
health.malaria_risk: Present below 1,700 m (5,600 ft) elevation; CDC records no malaria risk in Bogota, Medellin or Cartagena. CDC lists atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine or tafenoquine as prophylaxis options for at-risk areas.
health.notes: Three official sources state the yellow fever entry rule differently and this record does not pick silently between them. Colombia's Ministry of Health (Minsalud) states that under the International Health Regulations (2005) Colombia takes a non-restrictive position on yellow fever vaccination for people entering the country - it is not a blanket entry requirement - but that travellers going to Very High and High risk municipalities must be vaccinated 10 days in advance. Colombia's official tourism board says there are no mandatory vaccinations and recommends the yellow fever vaccine for certain areas. The UK FCDO says a certificate is required if arriving from certain countries with transmission risk. The US CDC's country page is the outlier and states the vaccine is required for all arriving travellers aged 1 year and over, while also noting it is not recommended for travel limited to Bogota or to areas above 2,300 m. The safe course is to carry a yellow fever certificate issued at least 10 days before arrival if you are coming from a risk country or going anywhere outside the high-altitude cities. Colombia's tourism board also notes some domestic routes (for example into the Amazon) ask for a yellow fever certificate at check-in. Water is described by the tourism board as generally safe to drink in large cities, with bottled water advised in rural areas and small towns.

money.card_acceptance: Colombia's tourism board states that in Bogota, Medellin, Cartagena, Cali and other regional capitals you can pay by card in most hotels, restaurants, shopping centres and tourist services, with Visa and Mastercard the most widely accepted and American Express and Diners Club less frequently taken.
money.cash_culture: Cash remains the most accepted method, especially in markets, small shops, public transport and rural areas. The tourism board advises carrying low-denomination notes (2,000 / 5,000 / 10,000 pesos) because many small businesses cannot break large bills, and recommends changing dollars or euros into pesos rather than trying to spend them - foreign cash is taken at exchange houses, not in shops.
money.atm_notes: Colombia's tourism board notes foreign-withdrawal commissions of roughly USD 3-5 per transaction plus surcharges for paying in another currency, and advises always choosing to be charged in Colombian pesos rather than your home currency when a card terminal offers the choice (dynamic currency conversion gives a worse rate). ATMs run 24 hours in major cities and shopping centres, many with an English-language option; it advises using machines inside banks or shopping centres.

power.adapter_note: Colombia's tourism board describes the common outlets as two flat pins, types A and B, as in the United States, and advises travellers from Europe or other 230V regions to bring a universal adapter and, where needed, a voltage regulator; both are sold in stores, airports and department stores.

emergency.notes: 123 is the single national emergency line and reaches police, ambulance and the fire service; 119 is listed separately for fire. These numbers are taken from the UK FCDO's Colombia travel advice rather than from a Colombian government page - Migracion Colombia and the National Police sites do not publish a consolidated emergency list that was reachable, and the US Embassy in Bogota's page returned 403 to an automated fetch. Bogota's city government describes Linea 123 as operating 24/7 with police and civilian operators dispatching police, the Bogota fire brigade and health-secretariat ambulances. No official source was found stating whether English is answered, and no tourist police number was verified, so that field is null rather than guessed.

getting_around.summary: Colombia is mountainous and large, so domestic flights (Avianca, LATAM, SATENA and others) are often the fastest way between regions and the only practical way to reach San Andres, Leticia, Nuqui or Cano Cristales; the tourism board advises booking one to two months ahead. An intercity bus network reaches virtually every city and town, with air-conditioned, wi-fi-equipped reclining-seat coaches on main routes - good value for medium distances, but mountain crossings take many hours and road conditions are worth checking in the rainy season. In cities, Bogota runs the TransMilenio articulated-bus trunk network plus the SITP local buses, and Medellin has the country's only metro, linked to the Metrocable gondolas serving the hillside neighbourhoods; Cali's MIO is a similar bus-plus-cable system. Taxis and ride apps are widely available, and in smaller cities like Pereira, Manizales and Bucaramanga transport is simpler and mostly cash.

passes.covers: TransMilenio trunk services and the SITP city buses in Bogota
passes.worth_it: Required rather than optional - Colombia's tourism board states you need the card to use the network. It is a stored-value card you top up, sold at system stations; it is not a time-limited tourist pass and there is no saving to calculate.

passes.covers: Metro de Medellin and connecting services including the Metrocable
passes.worth_it: Also a requirement rather than a discount product - the tourism board states you need the Civica card to use the system. Available at metro stations.

climate.precipitation_note: READ FIRST - this table is Bogota only, and Bogota is not Colombia. Colombia's official tourism board states there are no seasons in Colombia: climate is set by altitude and region, not by time of year, so temperatures barely move month to month and it is elevation that changes them. Bogota sits at 2,600 m and is cool all year (highs 15-17C); Medellin at about 1,500 m is mild all year; Cartagena on the Caribbean coast is hot and humid all year. Treat every figure below as a Bogota figure only - no verified month-by-month normals for Medellin or Cartagena were obtained, so no offset is given here rather than an invented one; pack for the altitude of each place you are going, not for the month. What does vary is rain: the Andean interior has two wetter periods (roughly March-May and September-November) and two drier ones. January itself is one of Bogota's driest months: 29 mm over about 8 rain days (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: Colombian school holidays run into mid-January, so domestic destinations and coastal flights stay busy in the first half of the month.

timezone_note: One zone nationwide; Costa Rica does not observe daylight saving time, so the offset from North American and European clocks shifts when those countries change.
passport_validity_rule: Costa Rica does not impose a six-month rule. The Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería's Directrices Generales de Visas de Ingreso y Permanencia para No Residentes set the minimum passport validity for first-group nationalities (which include the US, Canada, the UK, Australia, Brazil, Germany and most of the EU) at one day counted from the day of intended entry; the UK FCDO states the same rule as 'your passport must have an expiry date at least 1 day after the day you plan to leave Costa Rica'. Sourcing note: migracion.go.cr returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so the DGME wording here was read through search indexing of migracion.go.cr/visas/ rather than fetched first-hand, and the rule below is cited to the UK FCDO page that was read directly. Nationals in the second group (e.g. Belize, Bolivia, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras) face a longer minimum validity — check DGME directly if you hold one of those passports.
entry_requirement_notes: Costa Rica genuinely enforces onward travel at the border, not just at airline check-in: the official tourism board (ICT) states 'All travelers must therefore have a ticket for return or onward travel' — a pre-purchased bus or flight ticket, or cruise documentation, is accepted. Economic solvency is also a stated requirement: 'US$100.00 (one hundred US dollars) per month or partial month of legal stay in the country' (ICT, visitcostarica.com). Two official sources give different maximum stays and neither was overridden: the UK FCDO says 'You can visit Costa Rica without a visa for up to 180 days under a tourist visa waiver. The exact period is at the discretion of the immigration officer on arrival', while search indexing of migracion.go.cr/visas/ describes first-group nationals as admitted for up to 90 days — assume the officer's stamp governs and do not book non-refundable travel past the days actually granted. FCDO additionally notes a currency declaration for amounts of US$10,000 or more, a departure tax of about US$29 (usually included in the airfare), and overstay fines of US$100 per month.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever — required only for travellers aged 9 months and older arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines (MMR, Tdap, polio, varicella, influenza)
Chikungunya (per CDC, tied to an outbreak in the northwest)
health.malaria_risk: Present in the provinces of Alajuela and Limón; rare to no transmission elsewhere (CDC).
health.notes: Yellow fever is checked at the border, not merely advised. Costa Rica's Ministerio de Salud states that foreigners arriving from a risk zone who do not present the Certificado Internacional de Vacunación contra la Fiebre Amarilla to the immigration authority cannot enter the country ('los extranjeros que lleguen a Costa Rica y no presenten el Certificado Internacional de Vacunación contra la Fiebre Amarilla ante la autoridad migratoria, no podrán ingresar al territorio'). The Americas risk list named by the Ministerio de Salud is Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, French Guiana, Paraguay, Peru, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago and Venezuela, plus a set of African countries; CDC states the requirement applies to travellers aged 9 months and older. A separate and easily confused rule runs the other way: since 2026 Costa Rican citizens and residents departing Costa Rica for those same destinations must themselves be vaccinated at least 10 days before travel — that obligation does not apply to foreign visitors arriving. Neither the Ministerio de Salud article read here nor CDC stated a minimum number of days between vaccination and arrival for inbound foreign travellers, so no figure is given. Everything else listed under recommended vaccinations is advice, not a border check.

money.card_acceptance: The official tourism board states that all major credit cards are widely accepted and that US dollars are also widely accepted alongside the colón. No official source was found on where cards stop working, so assume cash for small rural businesses and buses.
money.cash_culture: Intercity buses are privately operated with no central terminal, and the tourism board advises bringing cash for lines that sell tickets only at the station — so carry colones for bus travel and small purchases even though cards are common.
money.tipping: Restaurant and hotel prices already include a 13% value added tax and a 10% service charge, per the official tourism board: an additional tip is optional and only for exceptional service, not expected.
money.atm_notes: The tourism board states ATMs are located throughout the country. No official source was found on fees, bank networks or dynamic currency conversion, so none is asserted.

power.adapter_note: The official tourism board specifies 110V outlets with standard US two-prong plugs (Type A). Grounded three-prong Type B outlets are also in general use but no official source confirmed that, so only Type A is listed. A traveller from a 230V country needs a plug adapter and must check that each device is rated for 110V — many hairdryers and kettles are not. Mains frequency is left null because no official source stated it.

emergency.notes: 911 is the single national emergency number. Costa Rica's Sistema de Emergencias 9-1-1 (operated by ICE) confirms nationwide 9-1-1 coverage, and the UK FCDO lists '911 (ambulance, fire, police)' for Costa Rica. No official source confirmed a separate tourist-police line or whether English is answered, so neither is claimed.

getting_around.summary: There is no national rail network for visitors and no countrywide transit pass. Intercity buses, run by several private companies rather than a government operator, reach nearly every popular destination cheaply, but there is no central terminal in San José — each line has its own terminal, and some sell tickets only at the station, for cash. Over ten domestic airports are served by Sansa and Green Airways, which is how travellers skip long drives between the Pacific coast, the Caribbean and the northern volcanoes. All of the above is as stated by the official tourism board; road-condition and drive-time claims are deliberately omitted because no official source was found for them.

timezone_label: EET (UTC+2) in winter, EEST (UTC+3) on daylight saving time — currently UTC+3
timezone_note: Egypt has a single nationwide time zone (IANA Africa/Cairo). Egypt's State Information Service states that Egypt reintroduced daylight saving time in 2023 after a seven-year hiatus and now runs it annually, clocks going forward on the last Friday of April and back at the end of the last Thursday in October. Daylight saving time is therefore in effect on this record's verification date (28 September 2026), putting Egypt at UTC+3; clocks return to UTC+2 at the end of October 2026.
passport_validity_rule: The UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office states: "To enter Egypt, your passport must have an 'expiry date' at least 6 months after the date you arrive and have at least one blank page." Egypt's own e-visa portal (visa2egypt.gov.eg) does not publish the rule on its public pages, so this is sourced from a foreign government's page about Egypt rather than first-hand from an Egyptian authority.
entry_requirement_notes: Per UK FCDO guidance on Egypt: most visitors need a visa, available as an e-visa applied for online through Egypt's official portal visa2egypt.gov.eg (valid up to 3 months) or as a visa on arrival at approved airports (30 US dollars in cash, up to 30 days); from 1 August 2026 a digital visa on arrival paid by card (36 US dollars) is available at Cairo International Airport. Travellers arriving by air at Sharm El-Sheikh and staying under 15 days within the designated resort area receive a free entry stamp instead of a visa. A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required if arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Amounts over 10,000 US dollars must be declared at customs. No proof of funds, hotel booking, travel insurance or onward ticket requirement is stated. This is a foreign government's summary, not a first-hand Egyptian citation — confirm against visa2egypt.gov.eg or an Egyptian consulate before travel.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever — certificate required only for travellers arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever virus transmission; not required for direct travel from the United States
recommended_vaccinations: Rabies (pre-exposure, depending on planned activities and access to medical care)
Routine vaccines (COVID-19, influenza, polio, DTaP, chickenpox, shingles)
health.notes: The only vaccination actually checked at the Egyptian border is the yellow fever certificate, and only for arrivals from a transmission-risk country (UK FCDO and US CDC agree on this). Everything else on the recommended list is advice, not an entry condition. The FCDO also notes HIV test results are required for work permits, not for tourist entry. Malaria risk is left null: the CDC destination page consulted carried no explicit malaria risk statement for Egypt and no other official source was reached, so no risk level is asserted here.

emergency.notes: The US Embassy in Cairo gives the Egyptian police hotline as 122, the tourist police as 126 and the ambulance service hotline as 123. No official source consulted confirmed a fire-brigade number, so it is left null rather than guessed. Note a genuine discrepancy in official guidance: Global Affairs Canada's Egypt page lists police 112, medical assistance 113 and firefighters 110 — if 122 or 123 do not connect, those are worth trying. Whether English is answered on any of these lines is not stated by any official source consulted.

getting_around.summary: In Cairo the metro is the practical way to cross the city; its state operator, Cairo Metro Company, runs the first, second and third lines and publishes fares and station lists on its own site. Intercity travel between Cairo, Alexandria and Upper Egypt is by Egyptian National Railways, which sells tickets through its official portal at enr.gov.eg. No nationwide tourist transport pass could be found on any official Egyptian source, so none is listed below.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Egypt's National Telecommunications Regulatory Authority (NTRA) requires every mobile line to be registered against an identified person's data, and enforces it — in August 2026 it referred all four Egyptian mobile operators to the Public Prosecution over lines registered under users' personal data without their consent. NTRA does not state on its site whether a visitor can register a line on a foreign passport, where, or what it costs, so none of that is asserted here.

climate.precipitation_note: About 4.1 mm across roughly 4 rain days.

climate.precipitation_note: About 5.7 mm — the wettest month on record at Cairo Airport, though that is still negligible rainfall.

timezone_note: Georgia uses a single time zone year-round and does not observe daylight saving time. The WMO station record for Tbilisi, supplied by Georgia's Department of Hydrometeorology, lists the zone as +0400 with DST = N; this agrees with the IANA zone Asia/Tbilisi (+04 all year). Note that the de facto authorities in Abkhazia and South Ossetia keep Moscow time (UTC+3); those regions are not accessible from the rest of Georgia and Georgian law treats entry to them from Russia as illegal.
passport_validity_rule: Georgia's national tourism board states that travellers from most countries need a passport valid for at least 6 months beyond their date of entry into Georgia, and that entry requires an ordinary or biometric national passport unless a treaty provides otherwise. Note: this figure is from georgia.travel (the official tourism board); the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' own consular site (geoconsul.gov.ge) is a JavaScript application that could not be read by automated fetch, so the MFA's wording could not be checked against it directly.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa-free stay is unusually long: Government of Georgia Ordinance No. 255 of 5 June 2015 (Legislative Herald of Georgia) provides that citizens of the countries on its list — 94 countries and territories, including the USA, UK, all EU member states, Canada, Australia and Japan — 'may enter Georgia without a visa and stay in the country for one full year' (i.e. 365 days per entry), not the 90-days-in-180 common elsewhere. Nationals not on that list may apply for an e-Visa at evisa.gov.ge; for an e-Visa the travel document must be valid at least 3 months beyond the requested visa's validity. The tourism board says proof of sufficient funds may be requested in some cases, that a return or onward ticket is 'recommended' rather than required, and that travel/health insurance is 'highly recommended' but explicitly not mandatory — so onward_ticket_required is recorded as false. No mandatory online arrival form or pre-registration was found.

required_vaccinations: None required for entry — the US CDC's Georgia destination page states that yellow fever vaccine is not required
health.malaria_risk: None — the CDC's Georgia destination page lists no malaria risk or malaria prevention guidance for the country.
health.notes: Nothing is checked at the Georgian border: the list above is travel-health advice, not an entry condition. The CDC page is a US government source used because no Georgian Ministry of Health page stating traveller vaccination advice in English could be located.

emergency.notes: 112 is Georgia's single emergency number for all services. The Public Safety Command Center 112, an entity of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, states that it takes calls 24/7 nationwide from landline or mobile with no prefix, and dispatches police, fire/rescue teams and emergency medical crews. Operators answer in Georgian, English, Azerbaijani, Armenian, Turkish and Russian. A free 112 Georgia app (Android and iOS) and a video-call/SMS channel for deaf and hard-of-hearing callers also exist. No separate legacy service numbers were confirmed by an official source, so none are listed here.

getting_around.summary: Georgian Railway runs the main intercity links, including fast trains between Tbilisi and Batumi on the Black Sea coast (train 802/801, roughly 5.5 hours: 08:00-13:35 westbound, 16:30-21:55 eastbound). Tickets go on sale up to 20 days before departure and can be bought at station ticket offices, at pay boxes, online at ticket.railway.ge or through the operator's mobile app; sales close 10 minutes before departure and a passport or personal ID number is required to book. Georgian Railway also operates international services. Marshrutka minibuses cover routes the railway does not, but no official source for their fares or schedules was found, so none are described here.

climate.precipitation_note: Mean monthly temperature 1.7 C; mean precipitation 18.9 mm over about 4 wet days — the driest month. Georgia's Department of Hydrometeorology supplies only mean monthly temperature to the WMO for Tbilisi, not separate daily maxima and minima, so avg_high_c and avg_low_c are null rather than estimated. Normals base period 1961-1990.
climate.crowd_note: Low season in Tbilisi; the ski resorts (Gudauri, Bakuriani) are at their busiest.

climate.precipitation_note: Mean monthly temperature 6.9 C; mean precipitation 30.3 mm over about 5.9 wet days. Mean-only data, 1961-1990 normals.

climate.precipitation_note: Mean monthly temperature 12.8 C; mean precipitation 50.5 mm over about 7.6 wet days — rainfall climbing steeply.
climate.crowd_note: Spring shoulder; comfortable in Tbilisi and the wine country, quiet before the summer influx.

climate.precipitation_note: Mean monthly temperature 21.2 C; mean precipitation 76.0 mm over about 8.7 wet days.

climate.precipitation_note: Mean monthly temperature 23.7 C; mean precipitation 47.5 mm over about 5.7 wet days.

climate.precipitation_note: Mean monthly temperature 19.6 C; mean precipitation 35.6 mm over about 5 wet days.

climate.precipitation_note: Mean monthly temperature 3.8 C; mean precipitation 21.0 mm over about 4 wet days.
climate.crowd_note: Low season in the cities until the New Year holidays; ski season starts in the mountains.

timezone_note: Indonesia spans three zones and none of them observe daylight saving. WIB / Western Indonesia Time (UTC+7, IANA Asia/Jakarta) covers Sumatra, Java — including Jakarta and Yogyakarta — and West and Central Kalimantan. WITA / Central Indonesia Time (UTC+8, IANA Asia/Makassar) covers Bali, Lombok and the rest of Nusa Tenggara, Sulawesi and South/East/North Kalimantan. WIT / Eastern Indonesia Time (UTC+9, IANA Asia/Jayapura) covers Maluku and Papua. This record uses WITA because Bali (Denpasar) is the single most likely arrival point for a visitor; if you are landing in Jakarta instead, set your clock an hour earlier to UTC+7. The WMO/BMKG station records confirm Denpasar at +0800 and Jakarta at +0700, both with no DST.
passport_validity_rule: Indonesia's Directorate General of Immigration requires a national passport valid for at least six months from the date of arrival. The official e-Visa portal states the passport biodata page must show "a minimum validity of 6 months from the date of your arrival to Indonesia", and the same six-month-from-arrival rule is stated for Visa on Arrival issued at the border.
entry_requirement_notes: Three things beyond the visa itself. (1) ALL INDONESIA ARRIVAL CARD — mandatory. Since 1 October 2025 every passenger arriving from abroad, regardless of nationality or visa type, must submit an arrival declaration through the All Indonesia system at allindonesia.imigrasi.go.id or the All Indonesia app. It is free, can be completed up to three days before arrival, and replaces the separate immigration, customs, health and quarantine forms (including the old electronic customs declaration). Only allindonesia.imigrasi.go.id is official. (2) BALI TOURIST LEVY — still in force. Every foreign tourist entering Bali pays a one-off IDR 150,000 levy under Bali Provincial Regulation No. 2 of 2025 (amending Regional Regulation No. 6 of 2023). Pay before or on arrival through the Bali provincial government's Love Bali portal at lovebali.baliprov.go.id, which issues a QR voucher; an exemption application route exists on the same portal. Copycat payment sites exist — use only the baliprov.go.id domain. (3) ONWARD TICKET AND FEES — Immigration states that VOA applicants must show a return ticket or a ticket onward to another country, and officers reserve the right to ask for a printed return ticket on arrival. Visa on Arrival / e-VOA costs IDR 500,000, permits a 30-day stay for tourism, and can be extended once for a further 30 days at an immigration office; it cannot be converted to another stay permit. Separately, bringing in more than IDR 100,000,000 in cash requires a customs declaration.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever — certificate required only for travellers arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from a non-risk country
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccinations up to date (MMR, DTaP, polio, varicella, influenza)
Japanese encephalitis (for some activities and longer stays)
health.malaria_risk: None in Jakarta or Ubud, and none in the resort areas of Bali and Java, the Gili Islands or the Thousand Islands (Pulau Seribu). Transmission is present in all eastern provinces (Maluku, North Maluku, East Nusa Tenggara, Papua, West Papua), in rural Kalimantan, West Nusa Tenggara, Sulawesi and Sumatra, and at low levels in rural Java.
health.notes: The yellow fever certificate is the only vaccination actually checked at the border, and only if you are arriving from a yellow-fever risk country — everything else on this list is medical advice, not an entry condition. A typical Bali or Jakarta trip needs no malaria prophylaxis. Note that a 2022 Immigration article on counter Visa on Arrival still lists a full-dose COVID-19 vaccination certificate among its requirements, while the current official e-VOA document list does not mention one; if you want certainty on that point, check evisa.imigrasi.go.id shortly before you fly.

money.card_acceptance: Visa and Mastercard are the most widely accepted and work at merchants across the major cities and tourist areas including Bali, Jakarta and Yogyakarta; JCB is accepted through BNI, CIMB Niaga, Mandiri and BRI affiliations, and American Express acceptance is limited, largely via Bank Danamon. Cards are reliable in hotels, larger restaurants and larger stores but not in warungs, markets or small local businesses. Shops do not always display which cards they take, so ask before ordering.
money.cash_culture: Carry rupiah in cash, especially outside the main cities — the national tourism board recommends withdrawing cash in a major city before heading anywhere remote. ATMs dispense IDR 50,000 or IDR 100,000 notes, and those larger notes can be hard to break in rural and non-tourist areas, so deliberately keep a stock of small notes. Notes in circulation run from IDR 1,000 to IDR 100,000. Bringing in more than IDR 100,000,000 (roughly USD 6,500) in cash must be declared to customs.
money.tipping: Tipping is discretionary rather than an obligation. Hotels and restaurants inside hotels operate a regulated service charge ("uang servis") added to the bill under Ministry of Manpower Regulation No. 7 of 2016, which requires that charge to be distributed to the staff — so where you see a service charge on the bill, the staff are already receiving it and a further tip is optional. No official Indonesian source sets a tipping percentage, and this record deliberately does not invent one.
money.atm_notes: ATMs on the Cirrus, Maestro and Plus networks are widespread in major cities and tourist areas. JCB cardholders can withdraw at affiliated bank ATMs (BNI, CIMB Niaga, Mandiri, BRI) and American Express cardholders at Bank Danamon ATMs. Machines dispense either IDR 50,000 or IDR 100,000 notes. No official source for per-withdrawal fees or dynamic-currency-conversion practice was available, so none is stated here — as everywhere, decline any ATM offer to bill you in your home currency.

power.adapter_note: Indonesia uses the two-pin European plug at 230 V / 50 Hz. Travellers from continental Europe and most of Asia need no adapter; UK (type G) visitors need a simple plug adapter only. Visitors from the United States, Canada and most of South America should check that their devices are dual-voltage (phone and laptop chargers usually are) and otherwise bring a voltage converter — the official tourism board advises exactly this. Adapters are sold in local minimarkets throughout Indonesia if you forget one.

emergency.notes: 112 is Indonesia's national emergency number, reachable from mobile and satellite phones, and is the number to use if you are unsure which service you need. Ambulance and medical emergencies can also be reached on 118 as well as 119. Two other numbers are worth saving: 115 for BASARNAS search and rescue (relevant for sea, diving and mountain incidents) and 129 for natural-disaster assistance. No separate national tourist-police number is published by the tourism board. Whether an English speaker answers is not guaranteed by any official source, so having your accommodation call on your behalf is often faster.

getting_around.summary: Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 13,000 islands, so moving between regions means flying or taking a ferry. The busiest gateways are Soekarno-Hatta (Jakarta), Juanda (Surabaya), I Gusti Ngurah Rai (Bali), Sultan Hasanuddin (Makassar) and Kualanamu (Medan), with connecting flights onward to smaller islands; PELNI runs multi-port inter-island ferries and ASDP runs single-route vehicle and passenger ferries. PT Kereta Api Indonesia (KAI) is the national rail operator, running intercity trains, Greater Jakarta commuter services and airport rail links, but its network covers Java and parts of Sumatra and does not extend to Bali, so getting around that island means ride-hailing, a hired car with driver, or a scooter. In cities, Damri buses serve the airports and metered taxis, ride-hailing apps, ojek (motorbike taxi) and bemo (minivan) fill in the rest. Indonesia has no nationwide tourist rail or transit pass — KAI lists no such product — so journeys are bought point to point.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Prepaid SIMs are sold from operator booths in the arrivals halls of the main international airports — Telkomsel, Indosat/IM3, XL, Smartfren, 3/Tri and Axis all have a presence. Registration is compulsory and the booth staff do it for you: a visitor registers with their passport, while residents use a KITAS or KITAP. eSIM does exist on Indonesian networks (Telkomsel sells prepaid eSIM starter packs), but Telkomsel's own prepaid eSIM registration page asks for an Indonesian KTP and family card, so a visitor is usually better off with a physical SIM registered against a passport at the airport, or an international travel eSIM bought before departure. Pocket wifi rental is offered as an alternative, orderable online for airport pickup or mailing. Free wifi is common at major airports, hotels, Jakarta train stations, malls, cafés and tourist sites.
connectivity.typical_cost: No official price list for a ~10 GB / two-week visitor bundle could be verified from an operator or government source, so none is invented here. For scale: the national tourism board states airport SIM prices "vary for each provider starting from IDR 10,000", and Telkomsel lists its SIMPATI eSIM starter pack (3 GB, plus call and SMS allowance) from IDR 25,000 (roughly USD 1.50). Checked 28 September 2026.

climate.precipitation_note: The wettest month: about 345 mm across roughly 27 rain days. Expect heavy, short downpours rather than all-day rain, plus high humidity.
climate.crowd_note: Busy through the first week for the New Year period, then noticeably quieter for the rest of the month.

climate.precipitation_note: Still deep in the wet season — around 274 mm over about 22 rain days, with humid, overcast stretches.
climate.crowd_note: One of the quietest months on the island; accommodation is at its most available.

climate.precipitation_note: Rain easing but still substantial, about 234 mm over roughly 20 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: Nyepi, the Balinese Day of Silence, usually falls in March. I Gusti Ngurah Rai airport closes completely for 24 hours from 06:00 WITA (medical evacuation and emergency landings excepted), and for that day nobody — visitors included — may leave their accommodation, with lights and noise restricted island-wide. Check the exact date before booking flights around it.

climate.precipitation_note: The switch to the dry season: rainfall drops sharply to about 88 mm over roughly 9 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: Good weather before the northern-summer rush arrives; prices and crowds are still moderate.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry season proper, around 93 mm over about 8 rain days, with lower humidity than the wet months.
climate.crowd_note: Arguably the best value of the year — dry weather without peak-season numbers.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry and a couple of degrees cooler: roughly 53 mm over about 6 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: Numbers climb through the month as the northern-hemisphere and Australian holidays begin.

climate.precipitation_note: Coolest and among the driest months, about 55 mm over roughly 4 rain days, often breezy.
climate.crowd_note: The busiest stretch of the year alongside August — book accommodation, drivers and popular restaurants well ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: The driest month of the year — only about 25 mm over roughly 4 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season continues; Indonesian Independence Day on 17 August brings nationwide celebrations and domestic travel.

climate.precipitation_note: Still firmly dry, around 47 mm over about 8 rain days, with temperatures starting to climb again.
climate.crowd_note: Crowds thin out after the school holidays while the weather stays reliable — one of the better windows.

climate.precipitation_note: Hot, with the rains returning late in the month: about 63 mm over roughly 12 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: Quieter than the mid-year peak; a good month if you can take the heat and occasional afternoon storms.

climate.precipitation_note: Wet season resumes in earnest, roughly 179 mm over about 16 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: A genuinely quiet month between the dry-season and Christmas peaks.

climate.precipitation_note: Very wet — around 276 mm over roughly 22 rain days, humid throughout.
climate.crowd_note: Wet and busy at the same time: the Christmas and New Year fortnight is one of the most crowded and expensive periods of the year, so this is a peak-price month rather than a peak-weather one.

timezone_note: Japan observes a single time zone nationwide, from Okinawa to Hokkaido, and does not use daylight saving time.
passport_validity_rule: Japan sets no minimum remaining validity beyond the trip itself: the passport only has to stay valid for the length of the stay. UK government entry guidance for Japan states "your passport must be valid for the length of your stay. No additional period of validity is required." JNTO's own visa page says only that all foreign visitors must hold a valid passport. Note that an onward airline or a transit country may still apply its own six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: Nationals of visa-exempt countries may enter for tourism for up to 90 days without a visa (JNTO; the exempt list is maintained by Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs). Visit Japan Web registration is not mandatory — JNTO states "Registration is not required, but advance registration makes procedures like tax-free shopping more convenient" — but Japan Customs requires every arriving passenger to make a customs declaration, and cash or other means of payment exceeding 1,000,000 yen must be declared. Practical trap: if you plan to use a Japan Rail Pass you need the "Temporary Visitor" stamp or sticker in your passport, and the automated immigration gates do not apply one — use a staffed counter or ask a clerk to stamp it.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccinations (MMR, diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis, polio, chickenpox, influenza, shingles)
Japanese encephalitis (longer stays or extensive rural/outdoor exposure)
Mpox (for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry to Japan — CDC lists yellow fever vaccine as both "not required" and "not recommended" for Japan, and its Japan destination page carries no malaria section and no antimalarial recommendation. Everything in the recommended list above is medical advice only; nothing on it is checked at immigration.

money.card_acceptance: International credit, debit and prepaid cards are generally accepted across the country and increasingly in shops and restaurants, and work for long-distance rail such as the shinkansen and the Narita Express. Short-distance train and subway fares typically cannot be paid by card, and smaller independent businesses may still be yen-only.
money.cash_culture: Japan remains, in JNTO's own words, "still very much a cash culture" — carrying some cash is recommended for the whole trip, and many smaller establishments accept only yen. A prepaid IC card (Suica, Pasmo) covers public transport, convenience stores and a growing number of shops, and is the usual way to avoid carrying coins, though it is not accepted everywhere either.
money.tipping: Not practised and best avoided. JNTO states "In Japan, it's not common to tip for services such as those provided in bars, cafes, restaurants, taxis, and hotels" and that tipping "can cause discomfort and confusion if you do." The one traditional exception is a gratuity called kokorozuke, which is given in an envelope rather than as loose cash; a private guide or interpreter used to overseas practice may also accept a tip.
money.atm_notes: Not every Japanese ATM takes foreign cards. The two networks JNTO names as accepting them are Japan Post Bank ATMs and Seven Bank ATMs in 7-Eleven stores (the latter offer 12-language menus). JNTO also warns that ATMs often charge for withdrawals, that many are not open 24 hours, and that they can occasionally run out of cash — so do not leave a withdrawal to the last minute.

power.frequency: 50Hz (eastern Japan, including Tokyo) / 60Hz (western Japan, including Nagoya, Kyoto and Osaka)
power.adapter_note: JNTO describes Japanese outlets as taking two flat parallel prongs (the Type A pattern) and states "The voltage used throughout Japan is uniformly 100 volts, A.C." Coming from a 230V country you need a plug adapter, and voltage matters more than the plug: dual-voltage devices such as phone and laptop chargers, hair dryers and shavers work nationwide, but any single-voltage 230V appliance needs a step-down transformer. Adapters and transformers are sold in electronics districts such as Tokyo's Akihabara and at major appliance retailers.

emergency.notes: JNTO lists only two numbers: 110 for police and 119 for fire or ambulance. No official Japanese source confirms that 112 reaches Japanese emergency services, so do not rely on it. For English-language help, the JNTO Japan Visitor Hotline on 050-3816-2787 runs 24 hours a day for emergencies such as illness and disasters, in English, Chinese, Korean and Japanese; the Tokyo Metropolitan Police English helpline is 03-3501-0110, also 24 hours, 365 days a year.

getting_around.summary: Almost every visitor moves by rail. The JR network plus the shinkansen links the major cities, city subways and private lines cover everything inside them, and a prepaid IC card (Suica or Pasmo) tapped at the gate is the simplest way to pay for short hops — short-distance rail and subway fares generally will not take a foreign credit card. Buses, ferries, domestic flights and taxis fill the gaps, and a rental car is mainly worth it outside the major cities.

passes.name: Japan Rail Pass
passes.covers: A joint product of the six JR Group companies giving nationwide travel on JR lines, with Ordinary Car and Green Car versions in 7, 14 and 21-day durations. Special conditions apply to the fastest NOZOMI and MIZUHO shinkansen services, which the pass does not simply cover.
passes.worth_it: An Ordinary 7-day pass is 50,000 yen through 30 September 2026 and 53,000 yen from 1 October 2026 (14-day 80,000 rising to 84,000; 21-day 100,000 rising to 105,000). JNTO's own guidance is that the regional passes are better value if you are staying in one area, so the nationwide pass really only pays off on a multi-region, long-distance itinerary.

passes.name: Regional JR passes (JR TOKYO Wide Pass, JR EAST PASS, JR-West, JR-Central, JR Kyushu, Hokkaido, ALL SHIKOKU, Hokuriku Arch)
passes.covers: Each covers one region — for example the JR TOKYO Wide Pass covers greater Tokyo including Mt. Fuji, Nikko and the Izu Peninsula, and the Hokuriku Arch Pass links Tokyo and Osaka via Nagano, Toyama, Ishikawa and Fukui.
passes.worth_it: JNTO states that regional passes offer better value than the nationwide pass when you are exploring a single area.

passes.name: Suica / Pasmo IC card
passes.covers: Prepaid tap-to-pay for public transport nationwide, plus convenience stores and a growing number of shops and restaurants.
passes.worth_it: Not a discount pass but the practical default for city travel and short hops, and the usual alternative to carrying cash. Not accepted absolutely everywhere.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Visitors can buy a prepaid SIM. JNTO's official Mobile Tips site states the handset must be SIM-free (unlocked) and must carry Japan's technical standards conformity certification mark for wireless equipment; nano, micro and standard SIM sizes are sold. JNTO points visitors to major airports, electronics megastores such as Bic Camera and Yodobashi Camera, and travel agencies. JNTO does not state any ID, passport or registration requirement for a prepaid tourist data SIM. Rented pocket Wi-Fi is the common alternative and is available at every major airport or by online reservation for hotel delivery; SoftBank's Free Wi-Fi Passport also gives two weeks of free access to about 400,000 hotspots.
connectivity.typical_cost: No official figure for a ~10GB / 2-week plan could be verified. The only price JNTO publishes is roughly 3,000 yen for a 1GB, 30-day data plan (checked 28 September 2026).

climate.precipitation_note: Tokyo's normal monthly precipitation is 59.7 mm. JMA notes that northwesterly winter winds leave the Pacific side sunny while the Sea of Japan side gets heavy snow.
climate.crowd_note: JNTO names 27 December to 4 January (plus adjacent weekends) as a peak period to avoid; from roughly the second week the month is one of the quietest of the year.

climate.precipitation_note: 56.5 mm — the lowest monthly normal of the year in Tokyo. Heavy snow continues on the Sea of Japan side, and inland Hokkaido regularly falls to around -20C.
climate.crowd_note: Falls outside all three of JNTO's named peak periods; among the least crowded months for visitors.

climate.precipitation_note: 116.0 mm. JMA describes spring as alternating cyclones and anticyclones with large short-term temperature swings.
climate.crowd_note: Demand builds sharply in the second half of the month as cherry blossom season starts: JNTO's 2026 forecast puts first bloom at 19 March in Tokyo, 24 March in Fukuoka and 26 March in Osaka.

climate.precipitation_note: 133.7 mm, with JMA noting increasing sunshine towards late spring.
climate.crowd_note: The busiest blossom weeks in Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka fall in early April, with Tohoku and Hokkaido following from mid-April (Sapporo forecast around 19 April). Golden Week begins 29 April — JNTO names 29 April to 5 May and adjacent weekends as a period to avoid.

climate.precipitation_note: 139.7 mm. JMA notes the rainy season already starts in early May in Okinawa and mid-May in Amami, well before mainland Japan.
climate.crowd_note: Golden Week (29 April to 5 May plus adjacent weekends) is a JNTO-named peak to avoid; after it, mid and late May is one of the best-value stretches of the year. Kushiro's late-blooming cherries are forecast around 5 May.

climate.precipitation_note: 167.8 mm. The Baiu rainy season begins in the Kanto/Koshin region around 7 June on the JMA 1991-2020 average — a cloudy, rainy early-summer period caused by a stationary front.
climate.crowd_note: No JNTO-named peak period; visitor numbers are low, largely because of the rain.

climate.precipitation_note: 156.2 mm. The Kanto Baiu ends around 19 July on average (JMA), after which the North Pacific High brings intense heat — western Japan regularly exceeds 35C.
climate.crowd_note: No JNTO-named peak until mid-August, but heat and humidity make long sightseeing days hard work.

climate.precipitation_note: 154.7 mm. JMA records August as the peak of typhoon formation (5.7 per month on the 1991-2020 average) and the hottest month.
climate.crowd_note: The week centred on 15 August (Obon) is a JNTO-named peak to avoid — domestic travel and transport are heavily booked. Combined with the heat and typhoon risk, this is the hardest month to visit.

climate.precipitation_note: 224.9 mm. JMA notes September brings heavy rain from the autumnal front and from tropical cyclones, with typhoon formation still near its annual peak.
climate.crowd_note: Outside all JNTO-named peak periods. Autumn colour begins in northern Hokkaido and the high mountains from late September.

climate.precipitation_note: 234.8 mm — the highest monthly normal in Tokyo, inflated by late-season tropical cyclones, though JMA describes October itself as generally sunny under frequent anticyclones.
climate.crowd_note: Outside all JNTO-named peak periods; comfortable temperatures and the start of the autumn-colour season working south from Hokkaido.

climate.precipitation_note: 96.3 mm — dry and settled in Tokyo, though JMA notes cold northwesterly flows and rising precipitation on the Sea of Japan side.
climate.crowd_note: JNTO calls November the best month to see autumn colour in most of Japan, so famous temple gardens and mountain areas get busy — but it is not one of JNTO's three named domestic travel peaks.

climate.precipitation_note: 57.9 mm — among the driest months in Tokyo, with heavy snow starting on the Sea of Japan side.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet and clear until about 27 December, when JNTO's New Year peak period (27 December to 4 January) begins and many businesses close.
