timezone_note: One zone nationwide. Visit Maldives (the national tourism board) states the country is '5 hours ahead of GMT', which agrees with the IANA zone Indian/Maldives at UTC+5 with no daylight saving. Note that many resorts run their own 'island time' one or two hours ahead of Malé time to give guests more daylight; that is a resort convention, not a legal time zone, and flights and ferries run on the national UTC+5 clock.
passport_validity_rule: Maldives Immigration requires a passport or travel document with a Machine-Readable Zone (MRZ) and at least one month's validity. There is no six-month rule. The UK FCDO states the same: the passport's expiry date must be at least one month after the date you arrive.
entry_requirement_notes: A free 30-day visa on arrival is issued to tourists of all nationalities (30-day figure per UK FCDO, used as a fallback because Maldives Immigration's own tourist-visa page does not state the length). Maldives Immigration requires, in addition to the MRZ passport: a confirmed return/onward journey ticket, sufficient funds to cover the stay (no figure is published) or a sponsorship approved by Maldives Immigration, and a prepaid confirmed booking at a registered facility. MANDATORY ONLINE FORM: 'All foreigners arriving in the Maldives must complete and submit the "Traveller Declaration" within 96 hours before arrival' via the IMUGA portal (imuga.immigration.gov.mv). A declaration is also submitted through the same portal for departure. Every traveller, including children and infants, needs an individual declaration, and it is free — Maldives Immigration warns that third parties have been charging for this free service, so use only imuga.immigration.gov.mv. Maldives Immigration also states that, since 15 April 2025, entry is not granted on Israeli passports. Customs: the UK FCDO notes it is illegal to bring in anything deemed contrary to Islam, including idols for worship, bibles, pork and pork products, and alcohol.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever - required for travellers aged 9 months and older arriving from, or with an airport transit or layover of more than 12 hours in, a country with risk of yellow fever virus transmission (CDC). Not required for travel direct from a country with no risk.
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines (MMR, polio, tetanus/diphtheria/pertussis, influenza, varicella, shingles)
health.notes: Yellow fever is the only vaccination tied to entry, and only on the arriving-from-a-risk-country basis above — everything else on the recommended list is medical advice, not a border check. CDC's Maldives destination page lists no malaria risk and recommends no malaria prophylaxis. CDC does flag dengue and chikungunya as mosquito-borne risks, so bite prevention matters more than pills here. Health care outside Malé is limited, and a resort in an outer atoll can be a long boat or seaplane journey from a hospital; medical evacuation is expensive, which is the practical argument for insurance, though the Maldives does not state an insurance requirement for entry.

money.card_acceptance: Visit Maldives, the national tourism board, states that 'all major credit cards are accepted in the country'. In practice that is strongest at resorts, Malé, and Velana International Airport; small guesthouses, cafes and ferries on inhabited local islands are the places to expect cash.
money.cash_culture: Resorts are effectively USD-denominated: rates, bills and extras are quoted and settled in US dollars, and the Foreign Currency Act 32/2024 (in force 1 January 2025) is built around that reality — it obliges resorts, integrated tourist resorts and resort hotels to exchange USD 500 per tourist per month, or 20% of gross monthly sales, into rufiyaa with a local bank (USD 25 per tourist for lower-tier tourist accommodation). The same Act requires domestic transactions generally to be conducted in Maldivian rufiyaa except where the law provides otherwise, so rufiyaa is what you need for ferries, local-island shops and taxis. Carry some rufiyaa for a local-island or ferry itinerary; a resort-only trip can be done almost entirely on a card in USD.

power.adapter_note: Visit Maldives states the supply is 240 volts. No Maldivian government or tourism-board page found states the plug type(s) or the frequency, so those are left null rather than guessed — check with your resort before you fly.

emergency.notes: The Maldives Police Service's own contact pages list 911 as the single emergency number, plus the police communications-centre lines +960 332 2111 and +960 332 2112 and a Tourist Police hotline on 1478. No current official Maldivian source found publishes separate ambulance or fire numbers, so both are left null rather than guessed — an older three-number set (119 police / 102 ambulance / 118 fire) circulates widely online but appears on no current government page, so treat 911 as the number to dial. Other official hotlines on the same page: Maldives Immigration 1434, Health Protection Agency 1676, Aasandha (health scheme) 1400, child helpline 1412. On a resort island, call the front desk or duty manager first — they coordinate the seaplane or speedboat evacuation that any real emergency will need.

getting_around.summary: There is no road network between islands and no railway — every journey is a boat or a plane. Visit Maldives describes the pattern: resort transfers are pre-arranged at booking, by speedboat for resorts near Velana International Airport and by seaplane or domestic flight for those further out, with several daily flights linking the country's domestic and international airports. Independent travel between inhabited local islands runs on the scheduled public ferry network from Malé to most of the atolls, which is cheap and slow and runs on a fixed weekly timetable rather than daily. In Malé itself, taxis serve the airport. Seaplanes fly in daylight only, so a late international arrival can mean an overnight in Malé or Hulhumalé before the onward transfer.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Visit Maldives states that prepaid SIM cards are available from two mobile service providers at the airport, usable for local and international calls and for data. No official source found states what identity document is required to register one.

climate.precipitation_note: About 114 mm. Northeast (iruvai) monsoon, the dry season, which the Maldives Meteorological Service puts at January to March.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season. Very busy and most expensive in the first ten days as the New Year period runs out, easing afterwards.

climate.precipitation_note: About 38 mm — by a wide margin the driest month of the year in Malé.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season, and the most reliable weather of the year. Book well ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: About 74 mm. Still dry-season conditions, with the sea usually calm and visibility good.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season. Prices start to soften late in the month.

climate.precipitation_note: About 123 mm. Transitional month; the hottest of the year and rainfall climbing towards the wet season.
climate.crowd_note: Shoulder. Still reliably sunny early in the month, with rates dropping as the month goes on.

climate.precipitation_note: About 219 mm. The southwest (hulhangu) monsoon, the wet season, normally begins in mid-May per the Maldives Meteorological Service — squally wind and short heavy downpours rather than all-day rain.
climate.crowd_note: Low season, with the year's sharpest fall in rates.

climate.precipitation_note: About 167 mm. Wet season, with the strongest winds of the year and choppier crossings.
climate.crowd_note: Low season. Quiet resorts and low prices; expect some lost afternoons to rain.

climate.precipitation_note: About 150 mm. Wet season, but a relative dip in rainfall between the May and August peaks.
climate.crowd_note: Shoulder. European summer holidays fill some resorts despite the season, so rates are not at their lowest.

climate.precipitation_note: About 176 mm. Wet season, plankton-rich water — the strongest months for manta ray and whale shark sightings in the western atolls.
climate.crowd_note: Shoulder. Northern-hemisphere holiday demand keeps prices up mid-month.

climate.precipitation_note: About 199 mm. One of the wettest stretches of the year.
climate.crowd_note: Low season and genuinely quiet, which is the trade-off for the rain.

climate.precipitation_note: About 194 mm. Still wet-season conditions; winds easing compared with mid-monsoon.
climate.crowd_note: Low season. Good value, with weather improving late in the month.

climate.precipitation_note: About 231 mm — the wettest month in Malé on the 1981-2000 normals.
climate.crowd_note: Low season until the very end of the month, when rates begin climbing towards Christmas.

climate.precipitation_note: About 217 mm, but falling fast through the month as the northeast monsoon sets in; the second half is usually much drier than the first.
climate.crowd_note: Peak from roughly 20 December. Christmas and New Year are the most expensive nights of the year and sell out months ahead.

timezone_note: The Ley de los Husos Horarios (in force 30 October 2022) sets four standard zones: Zona Centro (90 deg W, UTC-6) covering most of the country including Mexico City, Guadalajara, Oaxaca and Merida; Zona Pacifico (105 deg W, UTC-7) for Baja California Sur, Sinaloa, Sonora and Nayarit except Bahia de Banderas; Zona Noroeste (120 deg W, UTC-8) for Baja California; and Zona Sureste (75 deg W, UTC-5) for Quintana Roo, which is where Cancun, Playa del Carmen, Tulum and Cozumel sit. Daylight saving was abolished nationwide by that law; the only exception is a seasonal time in listed northern-border municipalities of Coahuila, Nuevo Leon, Tamaulipas, Chihuahua and the whole of Baja California, running from 02:00 on the second Sunday in March to 02:00 on the first Sunday in November.
passport_validity_rule: Mexico requires a passport or travel document that is valid for the whole period of your stay, with pages free for entry and exit stamps. No Mexican authority states a minimum validity beyond the stay - there is no six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: The paper FMM tourist card is gone for air arrivals. INM no longer issues a physical migration form to anyone entering Mexico by air: the Federal Migration Agent at the filter stamps the passport and records the estimated departure date, and the traveller can download the Forma Migratoria Multiple Digital (FMMd) once, within the days granted, by scanning the QR code at the checkpoint or via the INM services portal (inm.gob.mx/spublic/portal/inmex.html). At land border crossings the form still exists as the FMM Electronica: you complete it on the INM website, print it, and hand it over at the crossing point for the stamp. The stay is up to 180 days, but the exact number of days is at the immigration officer's discretion at the moment of entry - it is not automatically 180, and the number is what the officer records against the stamp. Mexican consulates state that officers may additionally ask a tourist for a hotel reservation and a return ticket, and the visitor condition requires economic solvency; these are discretionary checks rather than a blanket published requirement, so carry proof of onward travel and accommodation even though no rule mandates it. A visa is not needed for stays up to 180 days for nationals of the listed visa-exempt countries; separately, holders of a valid visa or permanent residence in the USA, Canada, Japan, the UK or any Schengen country may enter without a Mexican visa regardless of nationality.

recommended_vaccinations: Rabies (only for travellers with likely animal exposure)
Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTP, polio, varicella, influenza, COVID-19)
health.malaria_risk: Limited and localised - CDC reports transmission only in Campeche, Chiapas and southern Chihuahua, all P. vivax. No malaria along the US-Mexico border and none in the main resort and city destinations.
health.notes: Nothing is checked at the border: CDC lists no yellow fever entry requirement for Mexico, and Mexico's tourism ministry states no vaccinations are compulsory for most visitors, only that routine immunisations should be up to date. Chemoprophylaxis is advised by CDC only for the three malaria areas; elsewhere insect-bite precautions are enough. CDC also flags dengue, Zika, chikungunya and Chagas as insect-borne risks, a cyclosporiasis increase in travellers returning from Cancun and the Riviera Maya, and Rocky Mountain spotted fever in northern border states. Mexico City sits at about 2,300 m, so allow for altitude. Public and private hospitals are obliged to treat visitors regardless of nationality, and the tourism ministry recommends international travel insurance.

money.card_acceptance: No Mexican authority publishes a card-acceptance map, so treat card coverage as unverified outside established businesses and plan to carry pesos. What is official: Profeco requires businesses to state clearly which payment methods they accept and to take banknotes of any denomination, and it bans minimum-consumption conditions in restaurants and bars.
money.cash_culture: Mexico's tourism ministry says most visitors find it cheapest and most convenient simply to withdraw pesos from an ATM with an international card, with banks and casas de cambio in airports, cities and resort areas as the alternative. Paying in US dollars is explicitly discouraged - some tourist-area businesses take it, but at poor rates. The ministry also advises visitors not to carry large amounts of cash.
money.tipping: Expected, and by custom 10-15% of the bill in restaurants, bars and food stalls, plus loose change for porters, taxi drivers and cleaning staff. Legally it is always voluntary: Profeco states a tip is a voluntary gratuity that cannot be added to the bill without the customer's consent, no business may demand it or set the amount, and consumers can complain if they are made to pay one. Bargaining is normal in markets and on large purchases but not in fixed-price shops.
money.atm_notes: Using another bank's ATM carries a Mexican-side fee on top of anything your home bank charges. CONDUSEF's published range for a cash withdrawal at an ATM other than your card's issuer runs from about 8.62 pesos plus VAT at the cheapest bank to 40 pesos plus VAT at the most expensive, and fees are generally higher at machines in supermarkets, shopping centres, airports, bus terminals, convenience stores, pharmacies and petrol stations than at bank branches. By rule the commission must be shown on screen before you confirm, so read that screen and cancel if it is not worth it. CONDUSEF also advises checking the card reader for tampering, shielding the keypad, avoiding machines in poorly-chosen locations and keeping receipts.

power.adapter_note: Mexican official standards specify a 127 V single-phase supply at 60 Hz. Profeco's quality study of Mexican sockets and plugs shows the domestic socket as the North American duplex type - two flat parallel slots plus a round earth hole - and defines a clavija as an insulating body with two flat metal blades, with three-pin earthed plugs also sold. A traveller from a 230 V country needs both a physical adapter and a device that accepts 100-240 V; anything single-voltage 230 V will need a transformer, not just an adapter. Travellers from the USA and Canada need no adapter at all.

emergency.notes: 911 is the single national emergency number, dialable free from any landline or mobile anywhere in Mexico, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year; the call is routed by the Emergency Call Attention Centres to police, ambulance, fire or civil protection as needed. Whether the legacy 066 number or the European 112 still connect could not be verified from an official source, so dial 911. Separately, 078 is the national tourist assistance line run by the Secretaria de Turismo: its operators speak several languages and it handles tourist information, safety advice, contact with embassies and consulates, transport and accommodation questions, and can refer you to official bodies. It is an assistance line, not a police force. Major destinations also have visitor assistance units and Centro de Asistencia y Proteccion al Turista (CAPTA) offices.

getting_around.summary: Mexico is large and most long hops are done by plane or by long-distance coach - the tourism ministry rates the intercity bus network as one of the most extensive in Latin America and notes that the service level surprises many first-time visitors. Rail is limited but growing: the government-run Tren Maya links 34 stations across Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, Yucatan and Quintana Roo, including Palenque, Campeche, Merida, Izamal, Chichen Itza, Cancun, Playa del Carmen, Tulum and Chetumal, with tickets sold through its own reservation site. Within cities, Mexico City and Monterrey have metros, several cities have BRT corridors (Metrobus, Macrobus, Mexibus), and ride-hailing apps operate in most major cities and resorts; the ministry advises using authorised taxi desks inside airports rather than hailing on the street. Foreign driving licences are valid for car hire, federal motorways are tolled, and 'Hoy No Circula' plate-based driving restrictions apply in Mexico City, Puebla and Toluca.

passes.name: Tarjeta de Movilidad Integrada (Mexico City)
passes.covers: Mexico City's rechargeable transport smart card; the tourism ministry lists these city cards as accepted on the metro, city buses, Metrobus and other local transport services.
passes.worth_it: Get one on arrival if you plan to use city transport at all - it is the cashless way to pay across the network rather than a discount product. It is a city card only, with no value outside Mexico City.

passes.name: Mi Movilidad (Guadalajara)
passes.covers: Guadalajara's equivalent rechargeable transport card, accepted across local metro, bus and BRT services.
passes.worth_it: Only worth it if you are spending time in Guadalajara; each metropolitan area runs its own card and they are not interchangeable.

passes.name: Feria (Monterrey)
passes.covers: Monterrey's rechargeable transport card for the metro and local bus network.
passes.worth_it: Same logic as the other city cards - a local convenience, not a national pass.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: A prepaid Mexican SIM is cheap and easy to buy, and the tourism ministry recommends it over international roaming; your handset must be unlocked. Telcel, AT&T and Movistar all have national coverage, strong in cities and resort areas and patchy in remote rural areas. Free Wi-Fi is widely available in hotels, cafes, restaurants, airports, shopping centres and some public squares. Important recent change: guidelines published in the Diario Oficial on 9 December 2025 require every mobile line to be linked to an identified user before it works normally, and unlinked lines are disabled except for emergency calls once the transition deadline passes. Foreign nationals register with a passport (or a temporary CURP for foreigners), and providers record name, country of origin and passport number; biometrics, photographs and copies of ID are explicitly not stored. Expect to show your passport when buying or activating a SIM.

climate.precipitation_note: Deep in the dry season - about 12 mm over roughly 3 rainy days in Mexico City. Clear skies, cold mornings at altitude.
climate.crowd_note: Busy through Dia de Reyes on 6 January, then noticeably quieter. Pacific and Caribbean beach resorts are in their high season.

climate.precipitation_note: The driest month of the year in Mexico City - about 6 mm across 2 rainy days.
climate.crowd_note: Reliable weather and no major national holidays; among the easiest months to travel.

climate.precipitation_note: Still dry, about 12 mm. Warming fast, and haze can build over the central highlands late in the dry season.
climate.crowd_note: Spring equinox draws large crowds to archaeological sites such as Chichen Itza and Teotihuacan. Semana Santa can fall in late March, which fills domestic destinations.

climate.precipitation_note: The hottest month in Mexico City by average maximum, and still largely dry at about 24 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Semana Santa is the biggest domestic travel week of the year - beaches, colonial towns and coach routes all fill and prices rise.

climate.precipitation_note: The tourism ministry calls May the hottest month nationally, especially inland and in the north. Rain begins to return - about 59 mm over 11 rainy days in Mexico City. Eastern Pacific hurricane season opens 15 May.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet between Semana Santa and the summer holidays, but hot.

climate.precipitation_note: The wet season arrives properly: about 133 mm over 16 rainy days in Mexico City, typically as afternoon storms rather than all-day rain. Atlantic hurricane season opens 1 June.
climate.crowd_note: Low season inland; rain rarely stops sightseeing but afternoons need planning around.

climate.precipitation_note: About 174 mm over 22 rainy days in Mexico City - rain on most days, again mostly late in the afternoon.
climate.crowd_note: Mexican and North American school holidays fill beaches. Oaxaca's Guelaguetza, one of the country's great indigenous festivals, is in July and books out the city.

climate.precipitation_note: The wettest month in Mexico City at about 176 mm. Atlantic hurricane activity picks up sharply from mid-August on the Gulf and Caribbean coasts.
climate.crowd_note: Peak summer holidays continue. Guadalajara's international mariachi festival runs in August.

climate.precipitation_note: Still very wet at about 158 mm, and this is the statistical peak of the Atlantic hurricane season (10 September) - the highest-risk month for the Caribbean and Gulf coasts.
climate.crowd_note: Independence celebrations on 15-16 September are a nationwide highlight but also the busiest domestic weekend of the autumn.

climate.precipitation_note: Rain tapers off to about 71 mm over 10 days. Hurricane risk persists on both coasts until 30 November but eases through the month.
climate.crowd_note: Guanajuato's Festival Internacional Cervantino runs in October, and Day of the Dead celebrations begin around 28 October - book Oaxaca, Mexico City and Patzcuaro well ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry again at about 17 mm over 4 days, with clear, mild days and cool nights on the highlands. Arguably the best all-round month.
climate.crowd_note: Day of the Dead on 1-2 November is the single most oversubscribed few days of the Mexican calendar; after the first week the country empties out and the weather stays excellent.

climate.precipitation_note: The driest stretch of the year - about 5 mm. Cold mornings in Mexico City and the central highlands.
climate.crowd_note: Pilgrimages to the Basilica de Guadalupe on 12 December, then posadas and Christmas holidays from mid-month; beach resorts and flights are at their most expensive.

timezone_note: A change is in the air here and the official position is unsettled, so treat this as the one field to confirm on arrival. From October 2018 Morocco ran on GMT+1 all year under decree 2.18.855, dropping back to GMT for the whole of Ramadan each year — most recently from 03:00 on 15 February 2026 to 02:00 on 22 March 2026, announced by the Ministry of Digital Transition and Administrative Reform. On 25 June 2026 the Head of Government announced a decision to abandon GMT+1 and return to GMT 'starting the end of this summer' (official portal maroc.ma), and Moroccan press reports the switch took effect on 20 September 2026 — but no government page confirms that date, and the IANA time zone database, which is what actually sets the clock on your phone and on this page, still places Morocco at UTC+1. We show UTC+1 for that reason rather than following the press reports. The live clock above is computed from the IANA database, so it will follow the real change automatically once it is recorded there.
passport_validity_rule: A passport valid for at least three months beyond the date of arrival is required. Morocco's own consular site (consulat.ma) rejects automated requests, so this is taken from the UK FCDO's Morocco entry-requirements page, which states the requirement as agreed with the Moroccan authorities; Morocco's national tourist office states only that the passport must cover the duration of the stay. Many airlines apply a six-month rule at check-in regardless.
entry_requirement_notes: Tourist stays of up to 90 days are permitted without a visa for exempt nationalities; the Moroccan National Tourist Office says an extension of a further 90 days can be requested at the nearest police station. Nationalities that are not exempt apply for an e-Visa or AEVM electronic travel authorisation through Morocco's official portal acces-maroc.ma, or at a Moroccan embassy or consulate. The UK FCDO adds that foreign currency worth 100,000 Moroccan dirham or more must be declared on entry and on exit, that a damaged passport can be refused, that travellers should make sure they actually receive an entry stamp (people have had trouble leaving without one), that a polio vaccination certificate is required if arriving from a polio-affected country, and that private boats must arrive at a recognised port of entry.

required_vaccinations: Polio — certificate required only if arriving from a polio-affected country (UK FCDO)
health.notes: CDC lists no vaccinations as required for entry to Morocco; the only certificate requirement found is the conditional polio one noted by the UK FCDO for arrivals from polio-affected countries. Everything in the recommended list is advice, not a border check. CDC notes that rabid dogs are commonly found in Morocco. CDC's Morocco destination page carries no malaria prevention section, and NextStamp did not verify a malaria-free designation from WHO directly, so no malaria risk level is stated here rather than guessing one. The UK FCDO's Morocco health page says to dial 150 and ask for an ambulance.

money.card_acceptance: The Moroccan National Tourist Office states that Visa and Mastercard are accepted by most hotels and by some restaurants, shops and petrol stations — i.e. cards work in the formal tourist economy but not everywhere.
money.atm_notes: The Moroccan National Tourist Office says ATMs are widespread throughout Morocco, and that bureaux de change operate at airports, in hotels, in banks and in cities, with a passport required for exchange transactions. No official source was found for card fees or dynamic-currency-conversion practice, so none is stated.

emergency.notes: Morocco's Ministry of Health lists 19 for police and 15 for SAMU (ambulance) and the fire service, plus 022 25 25 25 for SAMU Maroc nationally. Note a discrepancy worth knowing about: the UK FCDO's Morocco health page instead tells travellers to dial 150 and ask for an ambulance. If one number does not connect, try the other. NextStamp found no official Moroccan confirmation that 112 reaches emergency services, and no official listing for a tourist police line, so neither is stated here.

getting_around.summary: ONCF, the national rail operator, runs what the tourist office calls Africa's second-largest rail network, linking Marrakech to Oujda and most major cities — though not Agadir, Nador or many smaller towns. The Al Boraq high-speed service currently serves four stations: Tangier, Kenitra, Rabat and Casablanca; tickets are sold at stations, on oncf.ma and through the ONCF Voyages app. Supratours coaches pick up where the railway stops. Within cities, petits taxis are colour-coded by city — red in Casablanca and Agadir, blue in Rabat, Tangier and Asilah, orange in Marrakech.

climate.precipitation_note: 25 mm on average — one of the wetter months in a dry city; cold nights.
26 mm on average; still a winter-rain month.
35 mm — the wettest month of the year on the 1991-2020 normals.
26 mm; showers still possible as the rains taper off.
10 mm; the dry season is setting in.
3 mm; effectively dry.
2 mm; the driest and hottest month.
5 mm; still extreme daytime heat inland.
15 mm; heat easing and the first autumn rain returning.
19 mm; warm days, comfortable nights.
30 mm; second-wettest month on the normals.
24 mm; mild days, genuinely cold after dark.

phrases_language: French (Morocco's de facto language of business, tourism, signage and menus alongside Arabic and Amazigh; a visitor gets further with French than with any other non-Arabic language, and it needs no romanization. Moroccan Arabic — Darija — is what people speak among themselves.)

timezone_note: Peru uses a single time zone nationwide and does not observe daylight saving time, so the offset is UTC-5 year round (IANA zone America/Lima).
passport_validity_rule: PROMPERU (the official tourism board) states that entry requires a legitimately issued passport with a minimum validity of six months from the date of entry into the country. The UK FCDO states the same rule for British nationals: the passport expiry date must be at least 6 months after the date of arrival.
entry_requirement_notes: Two official sources state the permitted stay slightly differently and both are worth knowing. PROMPERU (peru.travel) says the maximum stay granted is 90 days and that it cannot be extended; the UK FCDO says visitors are typically granted up to 90 days in any 180-day period, with a maximum of 183 days in any 365 days as a visitor. Plan around 90 days and confirm the figure written on your own entry record. Arrivals at international airports are registered digitally through the Tarjeta Andina de Migracion (TAM), a virtual immigration document - there is no paper form to fill in - but the FCDO notes that if you enter overland you must get a passport entry stamp at the immigration checkpoint yourself, and an overstay caused by a missing stamp is your problem at exit. Stays longer than 90 days, or travel for business, study or work, require the relevant visa from a Peruvian consulate before travel. Onward-ticket and proof-of-funds requirements are recorded as null: no page from Peru's own authorities that was reachable stated either as a border requirement, and asserting one on the strength of an aggregator would be a guess.

recommended_vaccinations: Typhoid (if visiting areas with poor sanitation or staying over a month)
Yellow fever (only for areas below 2,300 m in listed jungle/selva regions - not for Lima, Cusco city or Machu Picchu)
Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP/Tdap, varicella, polio, influenza, COVID-19)
health.malaria_risk: No transmission in Lima, Cusco, Machu Picchu, Lake Titicaca or anywhere above 2,300 m. Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for areas below 2,500 m east of the Andes, including Iquitos and Puerto Maldonado.
health.notes: Nothing is checked at the border: the US CDC states yellow fever vaccination is not required for entry to Peru, only recommended for certain low-altitude regions. The real health risk for a typical Peru itinerary is altitude, not disease. The CDC Yellow Book records Cusco city at 3,339 m (about 11,000 ft) and Lake Titicaca at 3,812 m (about 12,500 ft), and states that travellers going above 2,500 m (8,200 ft) are at risk of altitude illness - acute mountain sickness, high-altitude pulmonary edema and high-altitude cerebral edema. It specifically flags the Lima-to-Cusco flight, which gains roughly 3,350 m in about an hour, as an ascent rate that raises the risk, and notes that acute mountain sickness affects close to half of travellers during their first 48 hours in Cusco, though it is usually mild. CDC guidance is gradual ascent and, for travellers at risk, acetazolamide prophylaxis prescribed in advance - so this is a conversation to have with a doctor before booking, not after landing. Practical consequence for planning: do not schedule the Inca Trail or a high pass in the first day or two after flying into Cusco.

emergency.notes: These are the numbers published by the Presidencia del Consejo de Ministros on the Peruvian state platform: Central policial 105, Bomberos (fire) 116, and SAMU (mobile emergency medical service) 106. The same page lists Policia de carreteras (highway police) 110 and Defensa Civil 115. Two caveats it makes explicitly or by omission. First, SAMU on 106 is listed for Lima and for a named set of regions (Amazonas, Ancash, Ayacucho, Huancavelica, Huanuco, Junin, La Libertad, Loreto, Madre de Dios, Piura, Lima Region, Tacna, Tumbes, Ucayali, Lambayeque and Pasco) - Cusco is not on that list, so in Cusco or Puno expect to reach an ambulance through the police on 105 or directly through a clinic rather than through 106. Second, no single universal number and no tourist-police number is published on that page, so both are recorded as null rather than guessed; whether 911 or 112 connects is not confirmed by any official source found.

getting_around.summary: Distances are long and the Andes make roads slow, so most visitors fly between Lima, Cusco and Arequipa and then travel by road or rail locally; the Lima-Cusco hop is the one most itineraries are built around, and it is also the altitude jump that needs a rest day at the other end. In Cusco and the Sacred Valley, movement is by road (colectivo, bus or hired transport) plus the rail line to Aguas Calientes/Machupicchu Pueblo, which is the only way in other than walking. The part of a Peru trip that genuinely cannot be improvised is Machu Picchu itself: entry is capacity-capped by ministerial resolution, tickets are sold only by the state, and the popular dates go early.

passes.name: Llaqta de Machupicchu entry ticket (boleto de ingreso)
passes.covers: Timed entry to the Machu Picchu citadel on a specific date and circuit. Sold exclusively by Peru's Ministry of Culture through tuboleto.cultura.pe - the ministry's 2026 capacity resolution states sales are only through that portal, so any other seller is a reseller.
passes.worth_it: Not optional - you cannot enter without one. Entry is capped by ministerial resolution at 5,600 visitors per day on the specific high-season dates listed in the resolution and 4,500 per day for the rest of the year. The Ministry of Culture opened the whole 2026 season for advance reservation on 17 November 2025 (Machu Picchu reservations from midday), moving the opening forward from December to November specifically to avoid saturation on the busiest dates - so the realistic advice is to book as soon as the following year's window opens, and certainly several months out for June-August, rather than weeks out. Reserve on the portal and then pay on the same platform within the published payment schedule or the reservation lapses.

passes.name: Red de Caminos Inka permit (Inca Trail)
passes.covers: Trekking permit for the Inca Trail network into Machu Picchu, sold through the same official platform, tuboleto.cultura.pe, and only through a licensed operator.
passes.worth_it: Permit numbers are limited and the whole year opens for reservation on one day - for 2026 that was 17 November 2025, with Inca Trail reservations opening at 08:00, four hours before the Machu Picchu citadel tickets. Treat the trail as something you book the moment the window opens, up to roughly a year ahead, not something you add to a trip that is already dated. Hard constraint to plan around: the Ministry of Culture closes the entire Inca Trail network for the whole of February every year for maintenance and conservation, reopening 1 March, so a February trip cannot include it. Closures for heavy rain outside February have also happened.

climate.precipitation_note: Wettest month of the year in Cusco, 145 mm. Afternoon downpours are the norm and trail and road conditions suffer.
climate.crowd_note: Low season apart from a short New Year bump; the citadel is at its 4,500-a-day cap rather than 5,600.

climate.precipitation_note: Still deep in the wet season, 134 mm, with the heaviest sustained rain of the year around Cusco.
climate.crowd_note: Quietest month, but the entire Inca Trail network is closed 1-28 February for maintenance, so a trek-based itinerary is impossible.

climate.precipitation_note: Rain easing but still substantial at 107 mm; the landscape is at its greenest.
climate.crowd_note: Inca Trail reopens 1 March and is far less contested than mid-year.

climate.precipitation_note: Sharp drop to 43 mm as the wet season ends; clear spells return.
climate.crowd_note: Green scenery with dry-season skies arriving and far fewer people than June-August - arguably the best value month.

climate.precipitation_note: Effectively dry at 9 mm. Nights are getting cold at altitude.
climate.crowd_note: Dry-season conditions before the July-August crush.

climate.precipitation_note: Driest stretch of the year, under 2 mm, with warm days and near-freezing nights in Cusco.
climate.crowd_note: High season. Inti Raymi on 24 June fills Cusco; permits and hotels for that week go furthest ahead of anything else.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry, 4 mm, with the coldest nights of the year at altitude.
climate.crowd_note: Busiest month alongside August; expect the 5,600-a-day high-season cap and sold-out dates.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry at 9 mm; windy and dusty in the highlands.
climate.crowd_note: Peak of the peak. Book entry and permits many months ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: First light rains return, 22 mm, with mostly settled weather.
climate.crowd_note: Crowds thin noticeably after the northern-hemisphere holidays while conditions stay good.

climate.precipitation_note: Warmest days of the year in Cusco with rain building to 39 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Comfortable shoulder month; afternoon showers become likely.

climate.precipitation_note: Wet season arriving in earnest, 72 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet, and the month the following year's Machu Picchu and Inca Trail reservations open.

climate.precipitation_note: Back into heavy rain at 123 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Wet, but Christmas and New Year bring a short local and holiday-travel surge.

timezone_note: A single time zone applies to the whole country, including Palawan and Mindanao, and there is no daylight saving time.
passport_validity_rule: The Philippine government's official e-visa portal states that visa-free temporary visitors must hold passports "valid for at least six (6) months beyond the contemplated period of stay". A separate Philippine Embassy advisory on the post-Proclamation 297 entry and exit guidelines states the requirement as at least six months' validity at the time of entry. The stricter of the two readings — six months beyond your planned departure date — is the one recorded here.
entry_requirement_notes: Three things beyond the passport rule. (1) Onward travel: visa-free visitors "must also possess return tickets to their country of origin or outward-bound tickets to their next country of destination", per the official e-visa portal; the UK FCDO's Philippines page says immigration officials and airlines may ask to see it. (2) eTravel: registration in the Philippine One-Stop Electronic Travel Declaration System (etravel.gov.ph) is mandatory for all arriving passengers and is a prerequisite for immigration processing by Bureau of Immigration officers. It is free, can be done within 72 hours before arrival via etravel.gov.ph or the eGov PH app, and produces a QR code that airlines check at boarding and quarantine officers check on arrival. Diplomats, foreign dignitaries and their delegations, 9(e) diplomatic visa holders and diplomatic/official/service passport holders are exempt. (3) Visitors must have no derogatory record with the Bureau of Immigration. Most visa-free nationals get an initial 30-day stay; a few nationalities differ (Brazil and Israel 59 days; Hong Kong SAR and Indian passport holders without an AJACSSUK visa 14 days), so check your own nationality on the e-visa policy page. No proof-of-funds or mandatory travel-insurance requirement was found on any official Philippine source.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever (only if arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from a non-risk country)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP, polio, varicella, influenza)
Japanese encephalitis (stays of a month or more, or extended rural/outdoor exposure)
Rabies (for travellers with likely animal contact)
health.malaria_risk: Present in the province of Palawan and the Mindanao island group. Metro Manila and other urban centres are malaria-free. CDC advises prescription antimalarials for travel to risk areas.
health.notes: Only the yellow fever certificate is an entry condition, and only for arrivals from a yellow-fever risk country; everything else on this list is advisory and is not checked at the border. Dengue is a year-round mosquito-borne risk and the UK FCDO notes heightened dengue risk during the June-to-October rainy season, so insect-bite avoidance matters more than any vaccine for a typical short visit.

emergency.notes: 911 is the Philippines' national emergency hotline, covering police, fire and medical response. The UK FCDO's Philippines health advice tells travellers to "Call 911 and ask for an ambulance". The Department of the Interior and Local Government has been consolidating more than thirty separate local emergency numbers into this single nationwide 911 line. The Philippines' own emergency-hotline pages (e911.gov.ph, gov.ph/the-government/hotlines, officialgazette.gov.ph/emergency-hotlines) all return HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so the number here is cited to the UK FCDO's page about the Philippines rather than to a first-hand Philippine source. Whether 112 also connects, and whether English is reliably answered outside Metro Manila, could not be verified from an official source.

climate.precipitation_note: Deep in the dry season: 19mm normal for Manila. PAGASA classes December to February as the cool dry season, and January as the coolest month nationally (mean 25.5C).
climate.crowd_note: Busiest stretch of the year for foreign visitors; book Palawan and Boracay well ahead. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: Driest month in Manila's normals at 7.9mm. Still within PAGASA's cool dry season.
climate.crowd_note: Reliable weather and high demand; prices stay at dry-season levels. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 11.1mm in Manila. PAGASA's hot dry season runs March to May, so heat starts building.
climate.crowd_note: Good sea conditions with the heat still manageable. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: Manila's hottest average high (33.5C in the normals) with only 21.4mm of rain.
climate.crowd_note: Holy Week is the busiest domestic travel week of the year; beaches and inter-island ferries fill up. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: Rainfall jumps to 165.2mm as the dry season ends. PAGASA records May as the warmest month nationally (mean 28.3C).
climate.crowd_note: Hot and increasingly wet; the transition month, with rates starting to soften. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: PAGASA's rainy season begins: 265.0mm in Manila as the southwest monsoon sets in.
climate.crowd_note: Quieter and cheaper, but afternoon downpours and the first tropical cyclones disrupt island-hopping. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 419.6mm in Manila. PAGASA puts the peak of the typhoon season at July through October, when nearly 70% of typhoons develop.
climate.crowd_note: Low season; ferry cancellations and flight disruption are common. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: Wettest month in Manila's normals at 486.1mm, inside PAGASA's July-to-October typhoon peak. The Philippines averages about 20 tropical cyclones a year in its area of responsibility, 8 or 9 of which cross the country.
climate.crowd_note: The month most likely to have a trip rearranged by weather; Metro Manila flooding closes roads. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 330.3mm in Manila, still inside the typhoon peak.
climate.crowd_note: Cheapest fares of the year, but the least dependable for a fixed island itinerary. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 270.9mm in Manila. The last month of PAGASA's typhoon peak; rainfall starts easing late in the month.
climate.crowd_note: Improving toward month end, but still worth building slack into flight connections. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 129.3mm in Manila. PAGASA's rainy season formally runs to the end of November, but conditions improve markedly; late-season cyclones still occur.
climate.crowd_note: A good-value window before December rates rise. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 75.4mm in Manila as PAGASA's dry season begins; the cool dry season runs December to February.
climate.crowd_note: Dry, comfortable weather but a heavy domestic travel period around Christmas and New Year. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

timezone_note: Serbia has a single time zone and observes EU-style daylight saving. Per the IANA tz database for Europe/Belgrade, summer time (CEST, UTC+2) began 29 March 2026 and ends 25 October 2026, when clocks return to CET (UTC+1). Checked against the IANA database on 2026-09-28; the label above reflects the state on that date.
passport_validity_rule: Serbia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs states the passport must be valid at least 90 days after the intended date of departure from the Republic of Serbia, contain at least two consecutive blank pages, and have been issued within the past 10 years. This is a 90-days-beyond-departure rule, not a six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: Foreigner registration (the 'white card', prijava boravista stranca) is still in force: a stay must be registered with the police within 24 hours of arrival or of accommodation being provided. Hotels, hostels and other paid accommodation providers do this for you automatically; visitors staying in a private home or with friends are the ones who get caught, because the host (the person being visited) is legally responsible for registering them within 24 hours. Registration can now be done online through the eGovernment portal (euprava.gov.rs) instead of at a police counter, and the electronic confirmation is itself sufficient proof, so no paper slip needs to be carried. Holders of permanent residence have eight days rather than 24 hours. Separately, Serbia's MFA states that entry may be refused without sufficient funds, which it defines as 50 EUR per day of stay evidenced by cash or a bank statement; health insurance covering at least 20,000 EUR of medical costs is recommended but not mandatory; and border officers may ask to see a return ticket, though Serbia does not state an onward-ticket requirement as a condition of entry. Foreign nationals holding a valid Schengen, UK, EU member state or US visa or residence permit may enter, transit and stay up to 90 days in a six-month period without applying for a Serbian visa.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
Tick-borne encephalitis (for extensive outdoor or tick exposure)
Rabies (depending on planned activities and access to post-exposure treatment)
health.notes: Nothing is checked at the Serbian border: the CDC states yellow fever vaccination is not required for entry to Serbia, and the vaccines above are advisory only. CDC lists no malaria risk for Serbia. Tick-borne encephalitis is the one Serbia-specific item, relevant for hiking and rural outdoor time rather than city visits. The National Tourism Organisation of Serbia states that public mains water is safe to drink, and that all tourists have the right to emergency medical care during their stay.

emergency.notes: Police 192 and ambulance 194 are confirmed by the National Tourism Organisation of Serbia. Fire 193 and the pan-European 112 come from the UK FCDO's Serbia travel advice, used as a fallback because Serbia's own tourism and interior pages reached here did not list them; treat 193 and 112 as FCDO-sourced rather than first-hand Serbian citations. The tourism board also lists 1987 for AMSS roadside assistance. No official source consulted confirmed a dedicated tourist police line, so that field is null.

getting_around.summary: Serbia is compact and mostly covered by road: the government's own visitor portal describes roughly 1,000 km of motorway, putting Belgrade about an hour from Novi Sad and under two hours from most of the north and south. The headline rail service is the modernised 'Soko' high-speed train, which the same portal states runs Belgrade to Novi Sad in about 35 minutes with free Wi-Fi; tickets and timetables come from Srbijavoz, the national passenger rail operator. Within Belgrade, GSP runs more than 150 bus, tram and trolleybus lines plus over 20 night lines.

climate.precipitation_note: 46.9 mm normal; one of the drier months, but cold and often grey, with fog along the Danube and Sava.
climate.crowd_note: Lowest visitor numbers of the year outside the New Year period; Orthodox Christmas falls on 7 January.

climate.precipitation_note: 40.0 mm normal; the driest month of the year in Belgrade.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet in the cities; the Guca and Exit festival crowds are months away.

climate.precipitation_note: 49.3 mm normal; changeable, with the first genuinely mild afternoons.
climate.crowd_note: Still quiet and cheap; riverside kafanas and splavovi are only beginning to reopen.

climate.precipitation_note: 56.1 mm normal; showery but comfortable for walking.
climate.crowd_note: Pleasant and uncrowded; Orthodox Easter usually falls in April or early May and closes some businesses.

climate.precipitation_note: 58.0 mm normal; warm days with convective showers building toward the June peak.
climate.crowd_note: Arguably the best month to visit: warm, green, and ahead of the summer festival crush.

climate.precipitation_note: 101.2 mm normal, by a wide margin the wettest month; thunderstorms are common.
climate.crowd_note: Warm and lively; Novi Sad fills up sharply around the Exit festival in early July.

climate.precipitation_note: 63.0 mm normal; hot, with heat waves pushing well above the average high.
climate.crowd_note: Busiest month; Exit in Novi Sad and Belgrade's river nightlife are at full tilt.

climate.precipitation_note: 58.3 mm normal; the warmest month on the normals, and often dry and dusty in the city.
climate.crowd_note: Hot; many Belgraders leave town, so the city can feel emptier than the weather suggests. Guca trumpet festival draws large crowds.

climate.precipitation_note: 55.3 mm normal; warm days, cooler nights, generally settled.
climate.crowd_note: Excellent value: summer warmth without July prices or queues.

climate.precipitation_note: 50.2 mm normal; mild, with the year's best colour in the hills and national parks.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet and comfortable; clocks go back to CET on 25 October 2026, so evenings darken abruptly.

climate.precipitation_note: 55.1 mm normal; damp and frequently overcast, with persistent valley fog.
climate.crowd_note: Low season; indoor culture, kafanas and thermal spas are the draw rather than the weather.

climate.precipitation_note: 57.4 mm normal; cold and often wet, with snow possible in the city and likely on Kopaonik.
climate.crowd_note: Ski season opens at Kopaonik and Belgrade's New Year street celebrations are a genuine draw late in the month.

timezone_label: Sri Lanka Standard Time (UTC+5:30, no DST)
timezone_note: One zone for the whole island, offset by 30 minutes from whole hours and with no daylight saving. Half an hour ahead of Nepal-style offsets is a common mix-up; it is the same clock as India.
passport_validity_rule: The Department of Immigration and Emigration states as a general condition of entry that you must hold "a passport valid for a minimum period of six months from the date you arrive in Sri Lanka". The UK FCDO states the same rule for British travellers: the passport's expiry date must be at least 6 months after the day you arrive.
entry_requirement_notes: The Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) is a MANDATORY ADVANCE authorisation, not a visa on arrival. The Department of Immigration and Emigration states that "all foreign nationals, including nationals of the above-mentioned 40 countries ... are required to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) prior to arrival in Sri Lanka" (immigration.gov.lk/pages_e.php?id=60, and the same wording on eta.gov.lk). With effect from 25.05.2026 the tourist ETA is issued FREE OF CHARGE to nationals of 40 countries (including the USA, UK, Canada, Australia, India, China, Japan, Germany and France), plus Maldives, Seychelles and Singapore; the fee waiver does not remove the requirement to apply before travelling, and ETA fees paid before 25.05.2026 are non-refundable. The free tourist ETA is valid for 30 days from first arrival with double entry permitted (90 days for Maldivian nationals); longer stays require a paid extension through the immigration portal. Two further conditions are stated by immigration.gov.lk: a visit-visa holder must hold "a written assurance (ticket) to return to the country of domicile or a visa to the next country of destination", and Immigration must be "satisfied that you have adequate funds for your maintenance whilst in Sri Lanka and for the payment of your return passage" — no figure is published for what counts as adequate, so none is stated here. No blank-passport-page minimum is published by Sri Lankan immigration.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever — certificate required for travellers aged 9 months and over arriving from, or having transited, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from a non-risk country
recommended_vaccinations: Japanese encephalitis (for longer stays or rural/outdoor itineraries)
Routine vaccines including MMR and COVID-19
health.malaria_risk: None — WHO certified Sri Lanka malaria-free on 5 September 2016 and the WHO Sri Lanka country office reaffirmed ten years of sustained elimination in April 2026.
health.notes: Yellow fever is the only vaccination actually checked at the border, and only for arrivals from a transmission-risk country; everything in the recommended list is advice, not an entry condition. Sourcing conflict worth naming: WHO's certification and its 2026 follow-up are unambiguous that there is no local malaria transmission, while the CDC destination page still carries generic 'malaria is a risk in some parts of Sri Lanka, fill your prescription before you leave' boilerplate. The WHO certification is the better-supported position and is what the malaria_risk field reflects; a traveller who sees the CDC wording should know it is not a Sri Lanka-specific finding. Vigilance against re-introduction (imported cases) is a WHO theme, but that is a public-health programme concern, not a traveller prophylaxis recommendation.

money.card_acceptance: Sri Lanka Tourism states that most hotels, restaurants and shopping centres accept credit cards, and warns that some establishments illegally try to add a surcharge for paying by card. Outside those settings — small eateries, tuk-tuks, markets, rural areas — assume cards are not accepted.
money.atm_notes: Sri Lanka Tourism says it is easy to withdraw money island-wide at ATMs using international credit or debit cards. The UK FCDO is more cautious and is worth heeding: ATMs exist in major towns but not all of them accept international cards, most major banks allow Visa and Mastercard cash withdrawals, and bank card fraud is common — use ATMs inside a bank or hotel where possible and check the machine for signs of tampering. Bank hours are 0900–1300 Monday to Friday, with some city branches open until 1500 or on Saturday mornings.

power.adapter_note: Sri Lanka Tourism publishes the supply as "230–240 volts, 50 cycles AC" and advises bringing a stabiliser for laptops, but does not publish which socket types are in use, and no other Sri Lankan government source states them — so plug_types is left null rather than guessed. A traveller from a 230V country needs no voltage converter; the socket shape is the only open question and is worth checking with the accommodation.

emergency.notes: No Sri Lankan government source publishes a single consolidated emergency-number list that could be found, so the police and fire numbers here come from the UK FCDO's Sri Lanka travel advice — a foreign government's page used as a fallback, not a first-hand Sri Lankan citation. FCDO lists police as "118/119" (119 is given here as the primary; 118 is worth trying if it does not connect), fire and rescue as 111, ambulance as "011 2691111 or 1990", and tourist police as 011 2421052. Sri Lanka Tourism's own travel-tips page independently confirms 1990 for the ambulance service (the state-funded 1990 Suwa Seriya service) but gives a DIFFERENT tourist police number, +94 11 2382209, and adds a 1912 tourism hotline — both sets are reproduced here rather than one being picked silently. Whether 112 reaches an emergency operator in Sri Lanka was not confirmed by any official source, so universal is null. No official source was found confirming whether English is answered.

getting_around.summary: Sri Lanka Railways runs the intercity network and is the way most visitors cover long distances; seats can be reserved in advance through its seat-reservation system and the Pravesha smart-ticketing platform rather than only bought at the counter, and it markets scenic services such as the Ella Odyssey and Dunhinda Odyssey to tourists. Road transport (buses, hired cars with driver, tuk-tuks) covers everything the railway does not, but no official Sri Lankan source setting out fares, coverage or booking for those was found, so nothing is asserted about them here.

climate.precipitation_note: Northeast monsoon. The west and south coasts are in their dry half — Colombo averages only 58mm over about 5 rain days, one of its two driest months. The opposite is true on the other side of the island: the northeast monsoon is soaking the east and north, so Trincomalee, Batticaloa and Arugam Bay are wet and the eastern sea is rough.
climate.crowd_note: High season on the southwest and south coasts; the first week is still busy with the New Year tail. Editorial judgement, not a sourced measurement.

climate.precipitation_note: Driest month on the southwest coast — Colombo averages 73mm over about 5 rain days — as the northeast monsoon weakens. The east coast is still on the wrong side of that monsoon, though it is easing there too.
climate.crowd_note: Peak of the southwest-coast season; beach towns and whale-watching out of Mirissa are at their busiest. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: First inter-monsoon begins: rain arrives island-wide as afternoon and evening thunderstorms rather than as monsoon rain, and Colombo's total climbs to 128mm. This is the brief window when neither coast is monsoon-hit — the east is drying out while the southwest is still mostly fine.
climate.crowd_note: Still high season in the south and west but thinning after February. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: First inter-monsoon at full strength: 246mm in Colombo over about 14 days, almost all of it convective afternoon storms that clear. Hottest month of the year by daytime maximum. Both coasts are workable, which is unusual.
climate.crowd_note: Sinhala and Tamil New Year falls in April and domestic travel surges around it; transport and coastal accommodation get tight. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: The switch. Southwest monsoon onset makes this Colombo's second-wettest month (392mm, about 16 rain days) and hits the southwest coast and the hill country hardest — Sri Lanka Tourism describes it as heavy rainfall on the southwest coast and hills. Simultaneously the east and north dry out, and Trincomalee, Arugam Bay and Jaffna enter their good season.
climate.crowd_note: Southwest beach season ends; east-coast season begins. Low prices on the west, rising on the east. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Southwest monsoon established. Colombo's total drops sharply from May (185mm) but rain falls on about 16 days, so it is persistent rather than heavy, and the hills stay wet. The east coast is dry and settled — this is when Arugam Bay's surf season is running.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet on the southwest coast, building on the east. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Driest month of the southwest monsoon in Colombo (122mm) — the monsoon's rain is concentrated on the hills and the far southwest rather than the city. The east and north are at their driest and sunniest of the year.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season on the east coast and through the cultural triangle; European summer holidays add to it. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: As July: 120mm in Colombo, the southwest monsoon still running but at its least intrusive on the west-coast lowlands, and the east coast dry. The best single month to be on the eastern side of the island.
climate.crowd_note: Busiest month on the east coast and the second high season nationally. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: The southwest monsoon's tail, and Colombo's rainfall jumps back to 245mm over about 15 days. The east coast is still fair but its season is closing as the second inter-monsoon approaches.
climate.crowd_note: Thinning on both coasts; a genuine gap between the two high seasons. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Second inter-monsoon — the one time of year both coasts are wet at once. 365mm in Colombo over about 17 rain days, the highest rain-day count of the year, with heavy thunderstorms and squalls island-wide. Neither coast offers a reliable escape from the other.
climate.crowd_note: Lowest visitor numbers of the year and the widest choice of closed restaurants and hotels. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Wettest month in Colombo (414mm) as the second inter-monsoon runs into the onset of the northeast monsoon. Rain is widespread; the east and north are moving into their wet season just as the southwest starts to clear late in the month.
climate.crowd_note: Still low, though the southwest coast starts reopening towards the end of the month. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Northeast monsoon takes hold and the pattern flips back: Colombo drops to 175mm and the southwest and south coasts move into clear skies and calm seas, which Sri Lanka Tourism calls peak season there. The east coast is now the wet side.
climate.crowd_note: Southwest-coast high season restarts; Christmas and New Year are the most heavily booked fortnight of the year. Editorial judgement.

climate_reference_city: Colombo — on the WEST/SOUTHWEST coast, so this table tracks the southwest monsoon cycle. Sri Lanka's defining climate fact is that its two monsoons hit opposite coasts at opposite times: the southwest monsoon (roughly May–September) soaks the southwest coast and hills while the east and north are dry, and the northeast monsoon (roughly December–February) does the reverse. Averaging the island would erase this. Read the Colombo figures as the west/south coast, and each precipitation_note for what the east coast (Trincomalee, Batticaloa, Arugam Bay) and north (Jaffna) are doing at the same time. BASE PERIOD: the temperature and rainfall normals are 1961–1990, supplied to the WMO by Sri Lanka's National Meteorological Centre — that is the newest set the national met service publishes through WMO, so it is old but authoritative. Do not 'correct' it against a weather app.

timezone_note: The Tourism Authority of Thailand states the country's time zone as GMT+7; Thailand uses a single time zone nationwide and does not observe daylight saving.
passport_validity_rule: A passport must be valid for at least six months and have at least one blank page. The Royal Thai Embassy states the six-month validity requirement for entry under the Tourist Visa Exemption Scheme; the UK FCDO states the expiry date must fall at least six months after the date you arrive.
entry_requirement_notes: Since 15 September 2026 the visa exemption for nationals of 60 countries and territories (including the US, UK, Canada, Australia, Japan, India, Switzerland, New Zealand and all 27 EU member states) allows a stay of up to 30 days for tourism only — it replaces the previous 60-day scheme and no longer covers work of any kind. Immigration may extend it once by a further 30 days at its discretion. Entry via a land border checkpoint under this exemption is generally limited to two times per calendar year (Malaysian, Bruneian, Indonesian and Singaporean nationals are exempt from that limit). Seychelles and Mauritius get 15 days; Azerbaijan, Belarus and Serbia get Visa on Arrival. Proof of funds: the Royal Thai Embassy states travellers must possess adequate cash of 20,000 THB per person or 40,000 THB per family (note the UK FCDO quotes a lower 10,000 THB / 20,000 THB figure — carry the higher amount to be safe). The Thai MFA's visa Q&A lists a round-trip air ticket among visa-exemption requirements, and the FCDO notes you may be asked for evidence of onward or return travel. Separately, all foreign nationals must submit the free Thailand Digital Arrival Card (TDAC) at tdac.immigration.go.th; registration opens three days (72 hours) before arrival, with exemptions only for transit passengers who do not clear immigration and border-pass holders.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever (only if arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from the US, UK, EU, Canada or Australia)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP/Tdap, polio, influenza, chickenpox, shingles)
Japanese encephalitis (depending on duration and activities)
health.malaria_risk: Limited and localised. The CDC reports risk in rural and forested areas of the provinces bordering Myanmar, Cambodia and Malaysia, where atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline or tafenoquine prophylaxis is advised. There is no risk in Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai, Phuket, Koh Samui or Krabi province; in other transmission areas insect-bite prevention alone is recommended rather than medication.
health.notes: Nothing on this list is checked at the Thai border for an ordinary arrival — the only vaccination that can be demanded on entry is yellow fever, and only if you are arriving from a risk country. Everything else is medical advice, not an entry condition. Dengue, Zika and rabies are present; air pollution in Bangkok and Chiang Mai can be high, worsened by seasonal smoke haze. The UK FCDO warns that all Thai hospitals require a guarantee of payment before treating patients, so adequate health insurance is effectively essential.

money.atm_notes: Card and ATM fraud occurs. The UK FCDO reports incidents of ATM skimming and advises using an ATM inside a bank and always protecting your PIN. The Government of Canada advises using ATMs in well-lit public areas or inside a bank or business, avoiding card readers with irregular or unusual features, covering the keypad when entering your PIN, keeping your card in sight when it is handled by others, and monitoring statements for unauthorised transactions.

power.adapter_note: The Tourism Authority of Thailand states electricity runs at 220 volts with sockets compatible with European-style Type C or Type F plugs. A traveller from a 230V country (UK, EU, Australia, India) therefore needs no voltage converter — only a plug adapter if their plug shape differs. Travellers from 100-120V countries (US, Canada, Japan) need equipment rated for 220V or a converter; most modern phone and laptop chargers are dual-voltage, but check the label.

emergency.notes: Visitors should generally call the Tourist Police on 1155 first — the Tourism Authority of Thailand describes it as a 24-hour support line for travellers, and TAT also promotes a Thailand Tourist Police app. Whether 112 also connects to Thai emergency services could not be verified from an official source, and no official source was found stating which lines are answered in English.

getting_around.summary: The Tourism Authority of Thailand points visitors to tuk-tuks, songthaews and taxis, plus the BTS Skytrain and MRT metro in Bangkok, with domestic flights and long-distance trains and buses linking regions. Renting a car or motorbike is common but carries real risk: the UK FCDO reports a high number of road traffic accidents, particularly involving motorcycles, and warns that motorcycles and scooters hired in tourist areas are often unregistered and cannot legally be used on a public road. TAT advises checking road rules, licence requirements and insurance before driving, and notes that major airports now use biometric processing.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Visitors can buy a prepaid tourist SIM or eSIM on arrival. True (Thailand's largest operator, which absorbed dtac) sells Tourist SIM and Tourist eSIM products at True and dtac service centres nationwide, at airport counters open 24/7, and through its online store. A valid passport is required to register, in compliance with NBTC regulations, with a maximum of three SIMs per person per brand.
connectivity.typical_cost: 449 THB for an 8-day unlimited-data 'Tourist INFINITE' SIM from True, as listed on 28 September 2026; 15-day and 30-day versions are also sold but their prices were not published on the page, and a 10-day data-only variant exists. A USD equivalent is not given here because no exchange rate was verified against an official source.

climate.precipitation_note: The driest month in Bangkok — about 9 mm of rain on average. These are Bangkok (central Thailand) normals; regional variation across the country is significant.
climate.crowd_note: Core of the cool dry season and the busiest stretch for foreign visitors; book accommodation and domestic flights well ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: Still very dry, around 30 mm on average, with heat beginning to build.
climate.crowd_note: High season continues with comfortable conditions; northern Thailand can see agricultural burning haze late in the month.

climate.precipitation_note: About 29 mm — still dry, but daytime heat is noticeably stronger.
climate.crowd_note: High-season crowds start to thin as the heat rises.

climate.precipitation_note: The hottest month of the year in Bangkok, with about 65 mm of pre-monsoon rain.
climate.crowd_note: Songkran, the Thai New Year, falls in mid-April — TAT scheduled Bangkok celebrations across 9–15 April in 2026, with the main traditional dates 13–15 April. Expect heavy domestic travel, higher prices and some business closures around those dates.

climate.precipitation_note: The southwest monsoon arrives — rainfall jumps to roughly 220 mm, typically as heavy afternoon downpours rather than all-day rain.
climate.crowd_note: Low season begins; rates fall and sites are quieter.

climate.precipitation_note: Around 149 mm — a relative lull within the rainy season.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet and good value; humidity is high throughout.

climate.precipitation_note: About 155 mm, spread through the month.
climate.crowd_note: A secondary bump from European and regional summer holidays, but well short of the winter peak.

climate.precipitation_note: Around 197 mm as the monsoon strengthens again.
climate.crowd_note: Still moderately busy with summer-holiday travellers; expect wet afternoons.

climate.precipitation_note: The wettest month in Bangkok by a clear margin — about 344 mm. Flooding is possible in parts of the country.
climate.crowd_note: The quietest month for visitors, with the lowest prices, but the highest chance of washed-out days.

climate.precipitation_note: Still wet at roughly 242 mm, though the monsoon typically eases through the second half of the month.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet and inexpensive; conditions usually improve markedly toward month end.

climate.precipitation_note: Rainfall drops sharply to about 48 mm as the dry season sets in.
climate.crowd_note: High season restarts — arguably the best balance of dry weather and pre-Christmas crowd levels.

climate.precipitation_note: Very dry, around 10 mm, and the coolest month of the year in Bangkok.
climate.crowd_note: Peak of the season; the Christmas and New Year fortnight is the busiest and most expensive of the year.
