timezone_note: Türkiye uses a single time zone nationwide and has stayed on UTC+3 year-round since 2016 — clocks are not put forward or back for daylight saving, so the gap to European countries widens by an hour in their winter. Turkish diplomatic missions describe the country's time as GMT+3.
passport_validity_rule: Under Law no. 6458 on Foreigners and International Protection, a traveller's passport or travel document must be valid for at least 60 days beyond the 'duration of stay' granted by their visa, e-Visa, visa exemption or residence permit — not merely 60 days beyond the date of entry. Türkiye's Ministry of Foreign Affairs gives the worked example that a 90-day duration of stay requires 90 + 60 = 150 days of passport validity at the moment of entry, and a 30-day stay requires 90 days. The same ministry separately advises travellers to hold a passport valid for at least 6 months from arrival. NextStamp checks this as five months beyond your entry date (about 152 days): Türkiye ties the 60 days to the duration of stay you are *granted*, not to the day you actually leave, so measuring from departure would under-state the requirement on a short trip. Five months from entry matches how both the UK Foreign Office and Global Affairs Canada state it to their citizens, and clears the 150-day figure in the ministry's own worked example.
entry_requirement_notes: Most tourist visitors either enter visa-free or use the e-Visa obtained online at www.evisa.gov.tr; the e-Visa is valid only when the purpose of travel is tourism or commerce, and work, study or other purposes require a visa from a Turkish embassy or consulate. Many nationalities (for example British citizens) may visit for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Passengers arriving by cruise ship may enter without a visa for a maximum of 72 hours. Documentary filming, research and archaeological work require special advance permission from the Turkish authorities. No Turkish government source found states a proof-of-funds, accommodation-booking, travel-insurance or onward-ticket requirement for ordinary tourist entry, and there is no mandatory online arrival form. The 1-blank-page figure is as stated by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office for entry to Türkiye; Türkiye's own sites do not publish a blank-page rule.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccinations up to date (MMR, DTaP/Tdap/Td, polio, chickenpox, influenza, shingles)
Rabies (only for travellers with likely animal exposure through work or activities)
health.malaria_risk: Not clear-cut from official sources. CDC's Türkiye destination page states 'Malaria is a risk in some parts of Türkiye (Turkey)' but lists no antimalarial medicine in its Vaccines and Medicines table, and Türkiye does not appear on WHO's list of countries and territories certified malaria-free. Ask a travel clinic about your specific route rather than assuming either way.
health.notes: Nothing health-related is checked at the Turkish border for ordinary tourist arrivals — CDC states yellow fever vaccine is neither recommended nor required for entry to Türkiye, and the vaccines above are advisory only. Travel insurance covering local treatment and medical evacuation is strongly advised by several governments. Practical warning from the UK FCDO: foreign prescriptions are not accepted by Turkish pharmacies, and some medicines that are ordinary elsewhere are controlled in Türkiye — check with a Turkish embassy before travelling with prescription medication.

money.atm_notes: No official Turkish source was found covering ATM fees or dynamic-currency-conversion practice. The Government of Canada's travel advice for Türkiye advises using ATMs located inside a bank or business or in well-lit public areas, and covering the keypad with one hand when entering a PIN.

emergency.notes: Türkiye's Ministry of the Interior consolidated its separate emergency lines — 110 fire, 112 medical, 155 police, 156 gendarmerie, 122 AFAD disaster, 177 forest fire and 158 coast guard — into the single number 112, which was extended to all 81 provinces as of June 2021. 112 is the number the UK and Canadian governments both tell their citizens to dial in Türkiye (the UK FCDO says 'Dial 112 and ask for an ambulance'). No official source states whether calls are answered in English, so do not assume they will be; the gendarmerie (jandarma) rather than the police covers rural areas and much of the coast.

getting_around.summary: Türkiye's official tourism board describes high-speed trains, domestic flights, intercity buses and city subways as the practical ways to cross the country, calling the intercity bus network 'one of the most affordable ways to travel across Türkiye', with comfortable seats, online reservations and reasonable fares. Rail is run by TCDD (Turkish State Railways) and connects all major cities, with high-speed (YHT) lines running Ankara–İstanbul and Ankara–Konya. Within İstanbul, a single contactless card covers the municipal transport network.

passes.name: İstanbulkart
passes.covers: İstanbul's municipal public transport, including the Metro İstanbul rail network; it is the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality's transport and payment card, issued by Belbim.
passes.worth_it: Effectively required rather than optional — it is how you pay for city transport. Buy and top it up at the Biletmatik ticket-vending machines in metro stations on arrival.

passes.name: MuseumPass Türkiye
passes.covers: More than 350 museums and archaeological sites belonging to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, one entry per site.
passes.worth_it: Worth it only if you will visit several ticketed state museums and sites within its 15-day window, which starts at your first museum visit. Regional versions (MuseumPass İstanbul, Museum Pass Cappadocia) exist for shorter or single-region trips. It is not valid for Night Museology entries.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Turkish mobile lines are tied to the holder's identity document, and a device registered by a foreign visitor can only be used with GSM lines registered to that passport holder. The bigger trap is the handset, not the SIM: BTK (the Information Technologies and Communications Authority) allows a phone brought in from abroad to be used on a Turkish network for 120 days counted from your date of entry into the country, after which the device is cut off from Turkish networks unless its IMEI is registered — a paid registration made through the e-Devlet portal. A single short holiday is unaffected; long stays and repeat visits on the same passport are where people get caught.

climate.precipitation_note: One of the two wettest months in İstanbul (about 89 mm on the long-run average); cold, grey and occasionally snowy.
climate.crowd_note: Quietest time of year for the classic sights, with the shortest queues and the lowest room rates. Coastal resort towns are largely shut.

climate.precipitation_note: Still wet (about 71 mm) and still cold; snow in İstanbul and across the Anatolian plateau is normal.
climate.crowd_note: Low season continues. Cappadocia is atmospheric under snow but balloon flights are cancelled more often in winter weather.

climate.precipitation_note: Drying out slowly (about 62 mm); changeable, with cold snaps still likely.
climate.crowd_note: Shoulder season — cheap and uncrowded, but the weather is a gamble and some coastal hotels have not reopened.

climate.precipitation_note: Noticeably drier (about 48 mm) and mild; among the most comfortable months for walking cities and ruins.
climate.crowd_note: Excellent weather brings the first real crowds, and İstanbul's tulip displays draw visitors. Book ahead but expect shorter queues than midsummer.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry and warm (about 33 mm); reliable sunshine without summer heat.
climate.crowd_note: Arguably the best all-round month: the coast is warm enough to swim, inland sites are not yet punishing, and crowds are below the July–August ceiling.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry (about 28 mm) and hot; the Mediterranean and Aegean coasts are considerably hotter than İstanbul.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season is under way. Coastal resorts fill quickly and prices climb.

climate.precipitation_note: Driest stretch of the year (about 22 mm). İstanbul is hot and humid; inland and southern-coast temperatures run well above the İstanbul figures.
climate.crowd_note: Highest crowds and highest prices, overlapping with European school holidays. Sightseeing at Ephesus, Pamukkale or Cappadocia is best done at opening time.

climate.precipitation_note: Still very dry (about 24 mm) and as hot as July, with high humidity in İstanbul.
climate.crowd_note: The busiest month alongside July. Great for the coast, hard work for hot inland archaeology.

climate.precipitation_note: Warm and mostly dry (about 40 mm) as the summer heat eases.
climate.crowd_note: The other strong month: sea temperatures are still warm, the heat is manageable, and the family-holiday crowds thin after the first weeks.

climate.precipitation_note: Rain returns (about 66 mm) but days are still mild and pleasant.
climate.crowd_note: Good-value shoulder season. Coastal resorts begin winding down towards the end of the month; cities stay comfortable.

climate.precipitation_note: Wet (about 78 mm) and cooling fast.
climate.crowd_note: Low season. Cheap and quiet for İstanbul and Cappadocia; the coast is essentially closed for swimming.

climate.precipitation_note: The wettest month in İstanbul (about 99 mm), cold and often grey.
climate.crowd_note: Low season apart from a short New Year bump in İstanbul. Expect the shortest daylight hours of the year for sightseeing.

timezone_note: One time zone for all seven emirates. The UAE government fact sheet states "The UAE is 4 hours ahead of GMT" and Experience Abu Dhabi gives "+4 hours in front of UTC"; neither mentions daylight saving, which the UAE does not observe.
passport_validity_rule: The UAE government portal states plainly: "Passports must be valid for at least 6 months from the date of entry into the UAE." UK FCDO guidance for the UAE says the same for visitors — your passport's expiry date must be at least 6 months after the date you arrive — and adds that the requirement drops to 3 months for holders of a UAE residence permit.
entry_requirement_notes: MEDICATION IS THE THING THAT CATCHES PEOPLE OUT. UK FCDO guidance for the UAE states: "You will need approval from the UAE authorities to bring in medication that the UAE classes as narcotic, psychotropic, controlled or semi-controlled" and "You must get approval in advance from the UAE Ministry of Health to bring medication." On quantity: "You can bring up to 3 months' supply of medication as a visitor, reduced to one month's supply if the medication is included in the list requiring approval", and applications are "normally processed within 5 working days". The approving body is the UAE Ministry of Health and Prevention (MoHAP), which runs an e-permit service, "Issue of Permit to Import Medicines for Personal Use", and publishes the controlled/semi-controlled lists; mohap.gov.ae refused every automated request made during this research, so the rule above is cited to the FCDO rather than to MoHAP directly — check mohap.gov.ae yourself before travelling, and carry the original prescription and a doctor's letter regardless. Recreational and controlled drugs are a banned import outright (u.ae customs guidance lists "controlled/recreational drugs and narcotic substances" among prohibited goods) and the UAE enforces this severely. CASH: passengers entering or leaving with more than AED 60,000 (or the equivalent in other currencies) must declare it. VISA: many nationalities get a visa on arrival free of charge, but the permitted stay differs sharply by passport (for example FCDO states British citizens get up to 90 days in any 180-day period) and u.ae warns that "Lists of countries eligible for visa on arrival may vary from time to time" — check your own nationality before booking. Neither u.ae nor the FCDO states a proof-of-funds, hotel-booking, onward-ticket or travel-insurance requirement for visitors.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever (only for travellers aged 9 months and older arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for travel direct from the USA or Europe)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccinations (MMR, diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis, polio, chickenpox, influenza, shingles)
Rabies (only for travellers with likely animal exposure)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.notes: Yellow fever is the only vaccine tied to entry, and only conditionally: CDC lists it as not required for travellers arriving direct from the United States, and required for travellers aged 9 months and older arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Everything in the recommended list is medical advice only and is not checked at immigration. CDC's UAE destination page carries no malaria section and recommends no antimalarial drugs for the UAE.

money.card_acceptance: Experience Abu Dhabi (the emirate's official tourism board) states that "Credit and debit cards are widely accepted" and that "Most shops, hotels and restaurants in Abu Dhabi accept major credit and debit cards (Visa, MasterCard, American Express, etc.)", while advising you to "check before you order or purchase anything if there is no visible sign of card acceptance". Souks and smaller independent shops are the usual gap.
money.cash_culture: Cards cover most of a normal trip, but the tourism board's own advice is that "Carrying cash with you is recommended, as smaller shops or souks may not have access to a card machine", and that in souks and smaller shops "currency in smaller bank notes would be preferred". A few hundred dirhams in small notes is enough for most visitors; the dirham is pegged at USD 1 = AED 3.6725.
money.tipping: Not expected, but common. Experience Abu Dhabi: "Tipping is not expected but is commonly practised in the emirate. Gratuities to hotel and restaurant staff are at your discretion." Check the bill first — many fine-dining and high-end restaurants add a service charge of around 10% plus a 6% tourism levy, and menus say when those are already included. Where they are not included, the tourism board suggests 10-15%.
money.atm_notes: ATMs are everywhere — "in all shopping malls, major supermarkets, most petrol stations and the airport" — and accept American Express, Cirrus, Global Access, MasterCard, Plus System and VISA. Most are part of a central network, so a card from another bank works "for a nominal charge". For changing cash, the tourism board says bureaux de change "often offer better rates than the banks", while hotels exchange "at standard (non-competitive) rates"; a passport is required to exchange currency or travellers' cheques anywhere.

power.adapter_note: Sockets are the UK-style three-pin 13A pattern (Type G), so British and Irish plugs fit without an adapter and everyone else needs one. Two figures circulate in official UAE material: Ministry of Foreign Affairs country pages describe the domestic supply as 220 volts, while DEWA (Dubai's electricity utility) specifies its network as 230/400V at 50Hz. Either way anything rated 220-240V works unmodified; US 110V-only equipment needs a transformer, not just a plug adapter.

emergency.notes: The UAE government portal lists Police 999, Ambulance 998 and Civil Defence (fire) 997, callable from anywhere in the UAE, plus 991 for the electricity authority. For tourists specifically, u.ae gives Dubai Tourism Police on +971 50 453 8107 (the number in the field above) and Abu Dhabi Tourism Police on +971 2 800 2626 or +971 2 512 7777. English is widely spoken in the UAE, including by the emergency services, but no official page we could reach states a guaranteed language of response. We could NOT confirm from any official UAE source that 112 routes to UAE emergency services — dial 999/998/997 rather than assuming it does. Non-emergency government help is on 171 (Tawasul).

getting_around.summary: Most visitors split their time between Dubai and Abu Dhabi, which are linked by motorway and intercity bus. Dubai has a metro, a tram, public buses and traditional abras across the creek, all paid for with an RTA nol card rather than cash. Abu Dhabi has no metro: taxis are, in the tourism board's words, "reasonably priced and the most popular way to get around the city", alongside public buses, car hire and a free Visit Abu Dhabi shuttle bus available to visitors who book a hotel or buy attraction tickets in the emirate. Metered taxis and ride-hailing are cheap and plentiful in both cities and English is widely spoken by drivers.

passes.name: nol Silver card (Dubai)
passes.covers: All Dubai public transport modes — metro, tram, bus, water transport — plus some non-transport services such as parking
passes.worth_it: The default choice for a visitor staying more than a day or two: AED 25 including AED 19 of travel credit, valid for 5 years, and it is the only practical way to pay on Dubai's metro, tram and buses.

passes.name: nol Red Ticket (Dubai)
passes.covers: A single transport mode, on a disposable paper ticket
passes.worth_it: AED 2, valid 90 days or 10 trips. Only worth it if you expect to make one or two journeys; switching modes needs a new ticket, so the Silver card is better value for almost anyone staying a full day.

passes.name: nol Travel card (Dubai)
passes.covers: All Dubai transport services, bundled with tourist offers and discounts
passes.worth_it: AED 100 including AED 19 of credit — RTA markets it at tourists, but you are paying roughly AED 75 above the Silver card for the discount booklet, so only worth it if you will actually use the offers.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Visitors can buy a local SIM on a passport — TDRA's mobile-consumer registration policy allows visitors to register using a passport (or a GCC national ID) rather than an Emirates ID, for a limited period and up to two SIMs per service provider. e& (Etisalat) sells a prepaid Visitor Line at its business centres, outlets and partners on presentation of a valid passport and visa, in packs valid 28 days, with a maximum of two Visitor Line SIMs per passport. e& also offers a self-activated eSIM for visitors, activated by scanning a QR code and completing a facial-recognition step as soon as you clear immigration, which comes with 10GB of complimentary data valid for one day; du sells tourist prepaid plans as eSIMs too. Airport arrivals halls in Dubai and Abu Dhabi have operator desks.

climate.precipitation_note: About 11mm over roughly 2 rain days — one of the wetter months in an extremely dry year. (Figures throughout are the National Center of Meteorology's Dubai normals as published by WMO, base period 1974-1991.)
climate.crowd_note: High season. Experience Abu Dhabi calls November to April "the most pleasant time to visit", and hotel rates and beach-club demand reflect it — book well ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: Statistically the wettest month: about 36mm over roughly 4 rain days. Still sunny most days, but downpours are short and heavy and roads flood quickly.
climate.crowd_note: High season and very comfortable. Ramadan can fall in this month — its dates move about 11 days earlier each year, so check the current year before booking; during it, eating, drinking and smoking in public in daylight are restricted, some restaurants close or shorten daytime hours, and traffic is heavy just before sunset.

climate.precipitation_note: About 22mm over roughly 4 rain days, tailing off through the month.
climate.crowd_note: Arguably the best month: warm enough to swim, cool enough to walk. Still inside the November-April high season, and Ramadan or Eid al-Fitr may fall here depending on the year.

climate.precipitation_note: About 8mm over roughly 2 rain days; the last of the winter rain.
climate.crowd_note: The end of the pleasant season. Midday is already hot for sightseeing on foot, but evenings are excellent and rates start softening as the peak winds down.

climate.precipitation_note: Essentially dry — under 1mm on average.
climate.crowd_note: Outside the tourism board's recommended window. Rooms and flights get noticeably cheaper, but outdoor sightseeing is limited to early morning and evening.

climate.precipitation_note: No measurable rainfall in the normals.
climate.crowd_note: Deep summer. Everything worth doing is indoors and air-conditioned; nights stay above 26C, so even evenings are uncomfortable. Cheapest hotel rates of the year.

climate.precipitation_note: No measurable rainfall in the normals.
climate.crowd_note: The hottest month on record normals, with high Gulf humidity on top. Malls, museums and indoor attractions only; low rates, low crowds.

climate.precipitation_note: No measurable rainfall in the normals.
climate.crowd_note: As punishing as July and more humid. Many residents are away; hotels discount hard and shopping promotions run through the summer.

climate.precipitation_note: No measurable rainfall in the normals.
climate.crowd_note: Still summer in practice — the heat does not really break until October. Sea temperatures are at their warmest and least refreshing.

climate.precipitation_note: No measurable rainfall in the normals.
climate.crowd_note: The turn of the season: hot but bearable by late October, outdoor terraces and beach clubs reopening, and rates still below the winter peak.

climate.precipitation_note: Around 2mm; effectively dry.
climate.crowd_note: The official start of the pleasant season per Experience Abu Dhabi. Warm days, cool evenings, and the outdoor events calendar restarts — demand and prices climb through the month.

climate.precipitation_note: About 14mm over roughly 2 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: Peak of the peak: ideal weather and heavy Christmas and New Year demand. Expect the year's highest hotel rates and book restaurants and desert trips well in advance.

timezone_note: America/New_York is the Eastern zone — the one most visitors land in — but the country is not on one clock. The mainland spans four zones (Eastern America/New_York, Central America/Chicago, Mountain America/Denver, Pacific America/Los_Angeles), plus Alaska (America/Anchorage) and Hawaii (Pacific/Honolulu): six zones, and nine hours between Eastern and Hawaii in summer. Per NIST, daylight saving time runs 8 March to 1 November in 2026, beginning and ending at 2:00 a.m. local time (second Sunday of March to first Sunday of November); the IANA tz database agrees, putting America/New_York on EDT (UTC-4) today and switching it to EST (UTC-5) at 02:00 on 1 November 2026. NIST states DST is not observed in Hawaii, American Samoa, Guam, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, or the state of Arizona (except the Navajo Nation, which does observe it) — so Arizona is on America/Phoenix (UTC-7 year-round) and is an hour off its neighbours for half the year. Book domestic connections against the local zone, not a single national offset.
passport_validity_rule: U.S. Customs and Border Protection requires visitors to hold a passport valid for six months beyond the intended period of stay in the United States. Citizens of the countries on CBP's published exemption list (the 'six-month club') are exempt from that rule and need only a passport valid for their intended period of stay — the list is long and includes most of Europe, the UK, Canada, Australia, Japan, South Korea, India, Brazil, Mexico and Singapore. CBP's Carrier Liaison Program publishes the current list; the edition current for this record is dated 18 December 2025 and supersedes all earlier Carrier Liaison Program bulletins.
entry_requirement_notes: Entry is either visa-free under the Visa Waiver Program with an approved ESTA, or on a visa — and which one applies depends on nationality, not on the trip. CBP states the VWP covers citizens of 42 participating countries for tourism or business stays of up to 90 days; everyone else needs a visa from a U.S. embassy or consulate. ESTA must be approved before travel (air, sea or land), and CBP states an approval is normally valid for two years or until the passport expires, whichever comes first. The ESTA fee for fiscal year 2026, set by the inflation adjustment DHS published in the Federal Register on 19 November 2025, is $40.27 per travel authorization ($17 + $10.27 + $13); if the application is denied only the $10.27 system-cost component is charged. Apply only at esta.cbp.dhs.gov — third-party sites charge a markup. Onward ticket: 8 CFR 217.2(c)(1) requires VWP applicants arriving by air or sea to hold, at the time of arrival, a round-trip ticket carrying them out of the United States to a foreign port or place (a ticket terminating in contiguous territory or an adjacent island counts only if the traveller is a resident there). The same regulation says a round-trip ticket is NOT required of VWP applicants arriving at a land border port of entry, who must instead show the CBP officer evidence of financial solvency and a domicile abroad they intend to return to. CBP is explicit that an approved ESTA does not guarantee entry: admissibility is decided by the CBP officer on arrival.

health.notes: No vaccination is required to enter the United States as a short-term visitor. The one that was — proof of COVID-19 vaccination for non-citizen, non-immigrant air passengers — ended at 12:01 a.m. EDT on 12 May 2023, when the underlying presidential proclamation was revoked; the State Department's notice records that change. Fields left null rather than guessed: CDC's Travelers' Health destination pages exist for travellers leaving the United States, not arriving in it, so there is no official CDC recommended-vaccination list or malaria-risk statement for the USA as a destination to cite here. (Separate, stricter vaccination requirements apply to immigrant visa applicants and adjustment of status, not to tourists.)

emergency.notes: 911 is the single number for police, fire and emergency medical services anywhere in the United States — there is no separate number per service. The call reaches a local Public Safety Answering Point, which dispatches the right agency. Do not plan on 112: FCC consumer guidance states that 112 is an international/EU number and does not work in the United States, and that 911 is what you dial here. Sourcing caveat, stated plainly: fcc.gov returns 403 to automated retrieval, so the 112 point was read from search results quoting the FCC's own page rather than fetched first-hand; the safe instruction either way is dial 911.

getting_around.summary: There is no single national transport pass and distances are continental — most visitors fly between regions and get around locally by car or rental car. Amtrak is the national intercity passenger rail operator; its USA Rail Pass covers 10 segments over 30 days to more than 500 destinations in Coach class for $499, with the pass usable within 120 days of purchase and the 30-day clock starting on the first segment. Amtrak's separate California Rail Pass is no longer sold to new customers as of 26 August 2026, though passes already bought are still honoured. For anyone visiting federal parkland, the America the Beautiful annual pass is the one broadly worthwhile national pass. Practical framing (not from a cited source): outside the Northeast Corridor, rail is a scenic option rather than a fast one, and much of the West is difficult to reach without a car.

passes.name: America the Beautiful — National Parks and Federal Recreational Lands Annual Pass
passes.covers: Entrance fees and standard amenity (day-use) fees at federal recreation sites run by the National Park Service, U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, U.S. Forest Service, Bureau of Land Management, Bureau of Reclamation and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. Covers either one private vehicle fee or four per-person fees, depending on how the site charges. Valid one year from purchase.
passes.worth_it: $80 for U.S. residents, $250 for non-residents (NPS pricing as published, page last updated 5 January 2026). Only worth it if you will enter several fee-charging federal sites within the year — entrance fees vary site by site, so check the specific parks on your route before buying. Senior options are cheaper: $20 annual, $80 lifetime.

passes.name: Amtrak USA Rail Pass
passes.covers: 10 rides (segments) over 30 days, Coach class, to a choice of more than 500 destinations on the Amtrak network.
passes.worth_it: $499, which Amtrak frames as under $50 per segment — so it pays only if you actually use long, expensive legs rather than short hops. The pass is valid for 120 days from purchase, but once you start the first segment you have 30 days to finish the rest. Reservations are still required per segment.

climate.precipitation_note: 93mm. IMPORTANT: this whole 12-month table is New York City (Central Park) only — it is not a national average, and no such average would mean anything for a country that contains Alaska, Florida, Arizona and Hawaii at the same time. In the same January, Phoenix is mild and dry, Miami is warm, and interior Alaska is far below freezing. Use this column as the Northeast baseline and check the National Weather Service for your actual destination.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet after New Year; the cheapest month in most of the Northeast.

climate.precipitation_note: 81mm — the driest month in the Central Park record, but the snowiest (257mm / 10.1in of snow on average).
climate.crowd_note: Still low season in the Northeast; peak season in Florida, the desert Southwest and the ski states.

climate.precipitation_note: 109mm; snow is still normal (127mm / 5in average).
climate.crowd_note: Spring break pushes prices up in Florida, the Gulf coast and the Southwest for a few weeks.
Mild and not yet crowded in the Northeast; good desert and canyon weather before the summer heat.
Memorial Day weekend at the end of May is the unofficial start of the summer season — book ahead.
School holidays begin; national parks and coastal towns fill quickly.

climate.precipitation_note: 117mm — the wettest month in the Central Park record.
climate.crowd_note: Busiest and most expensive month nationally; Independence Day (4 July) is a major travel weekend.
Still peak; heat is the main constraint in the South and Southwest rather than crowds.
Crowds thin after Labor Day (first Monday) while the weather stays good — one of the best value months in the Northeast.
Autumn colour draws its own crowds to New England and the Appalachians; elsewhere it is quiet and pleasant.

climate.precipitation_note: 91mm.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet until Thanksgiving (fourth Thursday), which is the single heaviest domestic travel period of the year — avoid flying that week if you can.

climate.precipitation_note: 111mm, with 124mm / 4.9in of snow on average.
climate.crowd_note: Cold and quiet early in the month, then very busy and expensive from roughly 20 December through New Year.

timezone_note: One offset nationwide, all year. The IANA time zone database splits the country into Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh (south Vietnam) and Asia/Bangkok (north Vietnam), but both are UTC+7 and neither observes daylight saving, so the distinction never changes a traveller's clock.
passport_validity_rule: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months beyond the date you arrive in Vietnam, must carry at least 2 blank pages, and must be undamaged — travellers have been refused entry and exit over passport damage. You must enter and leave Vietnam on the same passport. Sourced from the UK FCDO's Vietnam entry requirements because Vietnam's own portals (evisa.gov.vn, xuatnhapcanh.gov.vn, travel.state.gov) refused automated access; Vietnam's national tourism authority separately states an e-visa applicant's passport must be valid 'for at least 6 months more'.
entry_requirement_notes: From 15 April 2026 all foreign nationals arriving at Tan Son Nhat Airport (SGN), Ho Chi Minh City are encouraged — not yet required — by the Vietnamese government to complete a digital arrival card online before arrival; the UK FCDO notes the scheme may change or extend to other airports, so check before you fly. The FCDO also warns you may be asked to complete a health declaration, which can include proof of vaccinations. Get your passport physically stamped on arrival. No proof of funds, onward ticket, accommodation registration or insurance requirement is stated in the entry rules. Separately, British citizens can visit visa-free for up to 45 days, and Vietnam's e-visa allows a 90-day stay with multiple entries.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines (MMR, influenza, polio and others)
Japanese encephalitis (depending on activities and length of stay)
health.malaria_risk: Rural areas only, with rare cases in the Mekong and Red River Deltas. No transmission in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, Da Nang, Hai Phong, Nha Trang or Quy Nhon.
health.notes: The US CDC lists no vaccination as required for entry to Vietnam, and states yellow fever vaccination is neither required nor recommended — nothing is checked at the border for a traveller arriving from a non-risk country. CDC recommends antimalarial medication for some specific provinces, and insect-bite precautions only in the Mekong and Red River Deltas. The UK FCDO notes dengue, Zika, Japanese encephalitis and malaria are all present, that many medicines sold locally are counterfeit or hard to find, and that Vietnam limits 'addictive' or 'psychotropic' medication to a 7-day supply without documentation — carry your prescription and a doctor's letter. Vietnam's national tourism authority advises bottled water and avoiding ice in rural areas, and says malaria risk is highest in the rural highlands.

money.card_acceptance: Hotels, tour operators, boutiques, restaurants, grocery stores and spas generally accept international Visa and Mastercard debit and credit cards, and Vietnam's national tourism authority says most larger travel expenses can be paid by card, on the spot or online in advance. Cash remains the norm for small purchases and street vendors.
money.cash_culture: Carry cash for street food, markets, small shops and anywhere rural — the tourism authority advises withdrawing extra before travelling to remote destinations, especially if buying crafts or textiles direct from artisans. Notes only, no coins, from 200₫ up to 500,000₫; mentally dropping three zeros makes the numbers manageable. Watch the 20,000₫ and 500,000₫ notes, which are similar shades of blue.
money.tipping: Not a normal part of Vietnamese culture and never obligatory — the tourism authority states there is no set rule. Tipping has become more common for private tour guides and in salons and spas; in restaurants and cafes it is not expected, though it is appreciated. A local meal costs roughly 30,000–40,000 VND, which is the benchmark the tourism authority suggests using to size a tip. Bargaining, by contrast, is normal in markets and casual shopping areas.
money.atm_notes: ATMs taking international cards are just outside arrivals at every major airport, and Visa is accepted at more than 20,000 ATMs nationwide. Per-transaction withdrawal limits are about 2–3 million VND at local bank ATMs and 5–10 million VND at international banks (the tourism authority's published list of higher-limit banks — ANZ, Citibank, HSBC, Commonwealth — is old enough that several of those have since scaled back retail operations in Vietnam, so treat the names, not the limits, as indicative). Conversion rates and swipe fees are set by your own card issuer. Note that buying US dollars once you are inside Vietnam is very difficult, so do not plan to reconvert.

power.frequency: 50–60Hz (as published by the US International Trade Administration; EVN publishes no figure in English)
power.adapter_note: Vietnam's national tourism authority states the supply is 220 volts and that most sockets take plugs with two round prongs (Type C); the Vietnamese Embassy in Washington also gives 220 volts. A traveller from a 230V country therefore needs only a plug adapter, not a voltage converter — and adapters are sold in any electrical shop, or lent by hotels. The tourism authority notes power cuts and surges are uncommon but do happen depending on location. Only the round-prong socket is officially described, so bring a Type C adapter rather than assuming a flat-pin plug will fit.

emergency.notes: These three numbers are published identically by Vietnam's national tourism authority and by the UK FCDO. There is no universal 112-style number: the FCDO lists 112 as national search and rescue and 111 as the child-protection hotline, not as general emergency lines. Critically, the FCDO states that emergency numbers in Vietnam are operated in Vietnamese only — if you can, have a Vietnamese speaker place the call. The FCDO also advises taking a translator when reporting a crime to police, and always obtaining a police report. No dedicated tourist-police number is published.

getting_around.summary: Vietnam is long and slow overland, and the national tourism authority openly recommends flying between distant cities — the Hanoi–Ho Chi Minh City train runs 30 hours or more (about 36 hours end to end on the Reunification Express), and central Vietnam to either end is commonly 16 hours. Domestic flights on Vietnam Airlines, VietJet and Bamboo Airways are cheap and frequent. A single 2,600 km north–south railway operated by Vietnam Railways carries five Reunification Express services a day in each direction, stopping at Hue, Da Nang, Nha Trang and Phan Thiet, with hard seat, soft seat, hard sleeper and soft sleeper classes; book days ahead normally, and two weeks ahead around Vietnamese holidays. Open-tour sleeper buses link the main tourist towns in the south and centre. Within cities, use metered taxis from the reputable operators (Vinasun and Mai Linh nationally, Taxi Group in Hanoi) or ride-hailing apps such as Grab, which require a Vietnamese SIM card to use; scooters rent for roughly 150,000–300,000 VND a day and bicycles for 20,000–30,000 VND.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Prepaid SIM cards are sold on arrival at major airports and from shops across the country. The three GSM operators are Viettel, Vinaphone and Mobifone, all with good coverage. You must show your passport to register the SIM. A Vietnamese number is also needed to use ride-hailing apps like Grab. Wi-Fi is widespread in cafes, hotels, shops and restaurants, with free public access in several tourist hubs and major airports.
connectivity.typical_cost: Vietnam's national tourism authority lists data-only SIM cards at 100,000–200,000 VND depending on the data included, and credit top-ups in 20,000–100,000 VND increments (page checked 28 September 2026). No official figure is published for a specific 10GB / two-week bundle, and no USD equivalent is published, so treat the VND figures as the sourced ones.

climate.precipitation_note: Hanoi's 28 mm falls as grey drizzle across about 11 days rather than downpours. Ho Chi Minh City is in its dry season at 12 mm; Da Nang still catches 83 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Tet, the Lunar New Year, falls in late January or early February — the tourism authority warns most businesses and restaurants close, and transport hubs overflow in the days beforehand. Book any transport well in advance.

climate.precipitation_note: The driest stretch of the year in both ends of the country: 19 mm in Hanoi, 8 mm in Ho Chi Minh City, 22 mm in Da Nang. Northern damp lingers as low cloud more than rain.
climate.crowd_note: The other half of the Tet window. If Tet falls in February, expect widespread closures and packed buses and trains around it.

climate.precipitation_note: 55 mm in Hanoi spread over roughly 18 drizzly days — frequent, light and grey rather than heavy. The south stays dry at 18 mm.
climate.crowd_note: The tourism authority describes northern Vietnam's cold season as running December to March, so March is the tail of it — pack a layer for Hanoi and Sapa.

climate.precipitation_note: 79 mm in Hanoi. The southern wet season has not started (57 mm in Ho Chi Minh City) and Da Nang is at its driest run of the year (50 mm).
climate.crowd_note: The tourism authority calls April and May sunny with a refreshing breeze in the north, but also warns those two months can be extremely hot elsewhere — the south sits at 34–35°C highs.

climate.precipitation_note: The rains arrive at both ends: 188 mm in Hanoi and 202 mm in Ho Chi Minh City as the southwest monsoon starts. Da Nang stays comparatively dry at 71 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Heat is the main constraint — the tourism authority flags April and May as potentially extremely hot.

climate.precipitation_note: Hanoi's hottest month and thoroughly wet at 231 mm over 16 days; Ho Chi Minh City 224 mm. Afternoon downpours are the pattern rather than all-day rain.
300 mm in Hanoi across about 18 rain days, 231 mm in Ho Chi Minh City. Hot, humid and the start of the northern typhoon window.
Hanoi's wettest month at 335 mm over 18 days; Ho Chi Minh City 219 mm; rain building in Da Nang at 167 mm.
Hanoi eases to 195 mm, but central Vietnam turns sharply — Da Nang jumps to 394 mm. The tourism authority warns central Vietnam gets storms and floods in the late rainy season.
climate.crowd_note: The tourism authority names September and October as favoured months in the north for cooler temperatures and clear skies.

climate.precipitation_note: Hanoi dries out to 126 mm over about 10 days — its best balance of the year. Central Vietnam does the opposite: Da Nang records its wettest month at 658 mm over 21 days, with flooding a real risk.
climate.crowd_note: Favoured in the north for cool, clear weather per the tourism authority — but a poor month to build an itinerary around Hue and Hoi An.

climate.precipitation_note: Hanoi's dry spell begins: 48 mm over about 7 days. Ho Chi Minh City drops to 128 mm as its wet season ends. Da Nang is still very wet at 486 mm.
24 mm in Hanoi and 41 mm in Ho Chi Minh City — dry at both ends. Da Nang still takes 272 mm over 21 days.
climate.crowd_note: The north is genuinely cold by now; the tourism authority puts northern Vietnam's cold season at December to March, so bring warm clothes for Hanoi, Sapa and Ha Giang while the south stays hot and dry.
